records.meaning: sukiyaki; Japanese hot pot, often with beef
records.difference: すき焼き is this named dish; しゃぶしゃぶ is another hot pot in which thin ingredients are briefly swished in broth.
records.filipino: sukiyaki; pagkaing hot pot na istilong Hapones

records.nuance: 焼く is transitive: a person applies heat to food. Here 魚を焼いています means someone is grilling or cooking fish now; it does not specify the method beyond cooking with heat.
records.logic: The を-marked fish is the object being cooked by someone.
records.meaning: cook; grill; bake; roast; burn (depending on context)
records.difference: 焼く is transitive (“cook something”); 焼ける（やける） describes it becoming cooked.

records.nuance: For grades/results, まあまあ gives a moderate assessment: acceptable or so-so, neither especially good nor bad. The Japanese sentence does not say the grades are excellent.
records.logic: It places the result around an adequate middle level rather than making strong praise or criticism.
records.difference: まあまあ is a middling assessment here; 良い（いい） gives a clearer positive evaluation.

records.nuance: 乾く is intransitive: moisture leaves the laundry and it becomes dry. すぐ means quickly, and 夏は sets the summer context.
records.logic: The laundry itself undergoes the change from wet to dry; no agent is stated.
records.difference: 乾く（かわく） is intransitive (“dry”); 乾かす（かわかす） is transitive (“dry something”).

records.nuance: 乾杯 is the conventional word for making a toast. Here the speakers propose a toast to the couple’s future; it is not simply an instruction to empty a cup.
records.logic: The characters can serve as memory cues, but the current word is an established toast expression rather than a literal description.
records.difference: 乾杯 is a celebratory toast; 祝う（いわう） means to celebrate or congratulate more generally.
records.filipino: Itaas natin ang baso para sa kinabukasan ninyong dalawa.

records.nuance: 乾かす is transitive: someone makes an item dry. The speaker dried the wet clothes; the sentence does not say whether this was by sun, air, or a machine.
records.logic: The clothes are the object being changed from wet to dry by an unstated agent.
records.difference: 乾かす（かわかす） takes the thing being dried; 乾く（かわく） describes the thing becoming dry.

records.kanji_breakdown: 新 = new; 幹 = main stem; 線 = line
records.nuance: 新幹線 is the name for Japan’s high-speed rail service and, in everyday use, its trains. The sentence says the speaker went to Kyoto by Shinkansen.
records.logic: The characters are useful cues, not a literal description; the established term refers to the high-speed rail system.
records.difference: 新幹線 is Japan’s high-speed rail service; 電車（でんしゃ） is the broader word for an electric train.
records.filipino: Shinkansen; mabilis na tren sa Japan

records.kanji_breakdown: マフラー = scarf wrapped around the neck
records.nuance: In this sentence, マフラー means a long scarf worn around the neck, commonly for warmth. The verb 巻く means to wrap/wind around.
records.logic: The surrounding phrase 首に and the verb まく identify the clothing sense, not a vehicle muffler.
records.difference: マフラー can also mean a vehicle’s exhaust silencer; here 首に巻く makes the scarf meaning clear.

records.nuance: 素晴らしい is strong positive praise. 素晴らしい景色ですね expresses admiration for the scenery; the sentence does not specify what makes it impressive.
records.logic: It evaluates the scenery as notably good or impressive rather than merely acceptable.
records.difference: 素晴らしい is strong praise; きれい can mean beautiful/clean but is less specifically an evaluation of overall excellence.

records.nuance: 海岸 is the land along the sea, such as a coast or seashore. 海岸を散歩する treats it as the route or area along which they will walk.
records.logic: The characters point to sea and shore; together the established word names the coastal area.
records.difference: 海岸 refers to the coastal land; 海（うみ） alone means the sea itself.

records.nuance: 家庭 refers to family life or the home as a family unit, not simply the physical house. In this sentence, he values his family/home life.
records.logic: The word conventionally describes the shared domestic life centered on a family; do not read it as a literal “house plus garden.”
records.difference: 家庭 emphasizes the home or domestic life; 家族（かぞく） more directly names the family members.

records.nuance: 庭 is the yard or garden around a home. The sentence says a rose was planted there; 庭 alone does not guarantee a formal landscaped garden.
records.logic: It names the open ground around a home where plants may be grown.
records.difference: 庭 is the garden/yard; 公園（こうえん） is a public park.

records.kanji_breakdown: アクセサリー = accessory; jewelry
records.nuance: アクセサリー is a broad word for an accessory worn with clothing, often jewelry. このアクセサリー is called lovely, but the sentence does not identify the item.
records.logic: It refers to an added item that complements clothing or appearance; the specific object depends on context.
records.difference: アクセサリー is broader than 指輪（ゆびわ）, which specifically means a ring.

records.nuance: 桜 can refer to a cherry tree or its blossoms. In the sentence with 咲く, it means cherry blossoms; March or April is a general seasonal statement and varies by region and year.
records.logic: The flowering context selects blossoms rather than the tree as an object.
records.difference: 桜 names the tree or blossom; 花（はな） means flower more generally.

records.nuance: 咲く is intransitive: flowers bloom. 桜の花が咲きました reports that the cherry blossoms bloomed; it does not say who caused them to bloom.
records.logic: The flower is the subject and undergoes the process of opening.
records.difference: 咲く（さく） is intransitive (“bloom”); 咲かせる（さかせる） means to make or cause something to bloom.

records.nuance: With 北風 as subject, 吹く means that the north wind is blowing. The sentence describes current weather; it does not state the wind’s strength.
records.logic: The wind is the moving air; 吹く describes that air movement.
records.difference: For wind, 吹く means “blow”; 風が止む（かぜがやむ） means the wind dies down/stops.
records.filipino: umiihip ang hanging mula sa hilaga

records.nuance: 散歩 is a walk taken at an easy pace, often for fresh air or exercise. The sentence says the grandfather takes one every day; it does not say how far or where.
records.logic: The word is conventionally used for going out on foot for a walk; the character cues are not a literal etymology.
records.difference: 散歩 is a walk/stroll; 旅行（りょこう） means a trip or journey.

records.nuance: あくび is an involuntary deep breath with the mouth open, often associated with tiredness or sleepiness. The sentence only states that the father yawned, so it does not establish why.
records.logic: It names the bodily action itself, without specifying its cause.
records.difference: あくび is the yawn; 伸び（のび） is a stretch, which can accompany a yawn but is a different action.

records.nuance: 植える is transitive: someone plants something in a place. Here a rose is planted in the garden; the agent is omitted in the Japanese sentence.
records.logic: The を-marked plant is placed into soil at the location marked by に.
records.difference: 植える（うえる） is transitive; 生える（はえる） describes a plant growing/emerging by itself.

records.kanji_breakdown: 屋 = house; 根 = root (character cue)
records.nuance: 屋根 is the roof or covering at the top of a building. In the sentence, a crow is perched/staying on the roof; it does not imply the bird landed just now.
records.logic: The compound names the building’s top covering; its meaning is established usage, not a literal “house root.”
records.difference: 屋根 is the roof; 天井（てんじょう） is the ceiling inside a room.

records.nuance: 黒板 is a board used for writing in a classroom or similar setting, traditionally dark and written on with chalk. The sentence asks someone to write an answer there.
records.logic: The characters describe the traditional black writing board; modern boards may have other colors or materials.
records.difference: 黒板 is for writing and teaching; 掲示板（けいじばん） is for displaying notices or information.

records.kanji_breakdown: 掲 = put up/display; 示 = show; 板 = board
records.nuance: 掲示板 is a place or board where notices and information are posted. The sentence asks whether the listener saw a notice there; it does not specify whether the board is physical or online.
records.logic: 掲示 means displaying/posting information; the full word denotes a notice board or bulletin board.
records.meaning: bulletin board; notice board; message board (context-dependent)
records.difference: 掲示板 is for posted information; 黒板（こくばん） is primarily for writing on during a lesson.

records.kanji_breakdown: からから = parched; very dry
records.nuance: When describing a throat, からから means extremely dry or parched. Here the throat became parched after chatting; it does not mean the throat made a rattling sound.
records.logic: The body part named with 喉が is described as having lost moisture.
records.difference: からから can also describe a rattling sound or something empty; 喉が in this sentence selects “parched.”

records.nuance: 草 is a general word for grass or other non-woody plants. In the garden sentence, plants are growing there; the wording alone does not prove they are unwanted weeds.
records.logic: 生えている describes plants growing/emerging; it does not add a negative judgment.
records.meaning: grass; plant; weed (when context indicates unwanted growth)
records.difference: 草 is general grass/plant growth; 雑草（ざっそう） specifically means weeds.

records.nuance: 葉（は） means a leaf. The sentence points to a particular leaf of a cherry tree; it does not refer to the blossom.
records.logic: The subject is identified as one leaf belonging to the cherry tree.
records.difference: 葉 is a leaf; 花（はな） is a flower.

records.nuance: 絵葉書 is a postcard with a picture or photograph on it. The sentence says one arrived from a friend; it does not say what image was printed on it.
records.logic: It is a kind of postcard distinguished by the image on it, not a different delivery method.
records.difference: 絵葉書 is a picture postcard; はがき can be a postcard without a picture.

records.nuance: はがき usually means a postal card. The sentence says the speaker is writing one to their family; it does not say it has a picture.
records.logic: The particle に marks the recipient; を marks the postcard being written.
records.difference: はがき is a general postcard; 絵葉書（えはがき） specifically has a picture or photograph.

records.kanji_breakdown: ふらふら = unsteady; weak or dizzy
records.nuance: With 疲れて, ふらふら describes feeling unsteady or weak from tiredness. The speaker may feel dizzy, but the Japanese does not diagnose a specific cause or condition.
records.logic: It describes the body’s unstable or weakened state; fatigue is explicitly given as context.
records.difference: ふらふら suggests loss of steadiness or strength; くらくら（する） more specifically describes a spinning/dizzy sensation.

records.nuance: 吸う means to draw air or another substance in. With 息を and 大きく, it means taking a deep breath in; the English “took a deep breath” conveys the whole inhalation naturally.
records.logic: 息を吸う is the act of inhaling; 大きく describes the breath as deep/full.
records.difference: 吸う means breathe in; 吐く（はく） means breathe out.

records.nuance: 普及 means becoming widespread or spreading widely. Here recycling of garbage has become common; the sentence does not say that every person recycles.
records.logic: The word describes something reaching many people or places, rather than a single person adopting it.
records.difference: 普及 means widespread adoption; 人気（にんき） means popularity or being liked.

records.nuance: 胃 is the stomach organ. 胃が痛い means the stomach hurts; から marks when the pain began, yesterday, and the sentence presents it as continuing.
records.logic: The stomach is the body part experiencing pain; it does not necessarily describe the entire abdomen.
records.difference: 胃 is the stomach; お腹（おなか） is the belly/abdomen more broadly.

records.nuance: 皿 is a shallow, flat dish for serving food. Here the cake is placed onto a plate; the sentence does not say whether it is one slice or a whole cake.
records.logic: に marks the plate as the destination surface, and を marks the cake being placed.
records.difference: 皿 is a flat plate; お椀（おわん） is a deeper bowl.

records.nuance: こぼす is transitive: someone spills or lets something spill out. Here wine ends up on the sofa; the sentence does not explicitly say it was accidental.
records.logic: ワインを marks what spilled, and ソファに marks where it spilled.
records.difference: こぼす is transitive (“spill something”); こぼれる is intransitive (“spill out”).

records.nuance: 血 is blood. 血が出ています says blood is coming out or that someone is bleeding now; it does not identify the body part or explain how it happened.
records.logic: The blood is the subject of 出る, literally “come out”; Japanese leaves the source unstated.
records.difference: 血 is blood; 出血（しゅっけつ） is the more formal word for bleeding/hemorrhage.

records.kanji_breakdown: 内 = inside; 容 = contain; form
records.nuance: 内容 means the contents or substance of something. この本の内容 refers to what the book says, and asks the listener to explain it; it need not mean a short summary.
records.logic: The book is the container/topic, and 内容 is the information within it.
records.difference: 内容 is the material or information in something; 目次（もくじ） is its table of contents.

records.nuance: 背景 means background. With 事件の and 何があった, it refers to circumstances or factors behind the incident, not a visible scenic backdrop.
records.logic: The question asks what circumstances lay behind the incident; it does not imply a hidden culprit or conspiracy.
records.difference: 背景 can mean underlying circumstances; 原因（げんいん） means a cause and is more direct.
records.filipino: mga pangyayaring nasa likod ng insidente

records.nuance: 骨 is a bone. 足の骨 means a bone in the foot/leg area; the sentence says it was broken but does not identify which bone.
records.logic: The phrase 骨を折る here is literal because 足の骨 is specified; it means fracture a bone, not idiomatic “make an effort.”
records.difference: 骨 is an individual bone; 骨格（こっかく） is the skeleton or supporting framework.

records.nuance: In this context, ランチ means lunch or a midday meal. 一緒にランチに行く is an invitation to go eat lunch together; it does not specify a restaurant or menu.
records.logic: ランチに行く is a common way to say go out for lunch.
records.difference: ランチ is lunch; 夕食（ゆうしょく） is the evening meal.

records.nuance: 滑る means to slide or slip over a surface. Here he moved over the snow; the sentence does not say that he fell or was injured.
records.logic: 雪の上を marks the surface traversed; no destination or cause is stated.
records.difference: 滑る describes sliding movement; 転ぶ（ころぶ） means to fall over.

records.nuance: 折れる is intransitive: the branch breaks under the strong wind. It does not say who broke it intentionally.
records.logic: 木の枝が is the thing undergoing the break; 強風で gives the force or circumstance.
records.difference: 折れる is intransitive (“break”); 折る（おる） is transitive (“break something”).

records.nuance: 折る is transitive: someone breaks or fractures something. 足の骨を折る means to break a bone in the foot/leg; it does not use the idiomatic “make an effort” sense of 骨を折る.
records.logic: 足の骨 is the object of 折る; the agent is identified as the grandfather.
records.difference: 折る is transitive (“break something”); 折れる（おれる） says the thing breaks by itself or under a force.
records.filipino: nabali ang buto niya sa paa

records.nuance: 健康 means health or being healthy. 健康な生活 is a healthy way of life; it does not claim the speaker never becomes ill.
records.logic: 健康な modifies 生活, describing a lifestyle that supports well-being.
records.difference: 健康 describes good physical or mental condition; 元気（げんき） often emphasizes energy or feeling lively.

records.nuance: レシート is a receipt, usually the printed record of a purchase. The sentence says it was put in a wallet; it does not state what was bought.
records.logic: 財布に marks where the receipt was put; the item is not necessarily a formal invoice.
records.difference: レシート is the purchase receipt; 領収書（りょうしゅうしょ） is a receipt/official proof of payment and can be more formal.

records.nuance: 珍しい means uncommon or unusual. The fruit was not something the speaker often encounters; the sentence does not necessarily mean it tasted strange or bad.
records.logic: It evaluates how rarely encountered or how unfamiliar the fruit is, not its flavor.
records.difference: 珍しい describes rarity or unfamiliarity; 変な（へんな） more directly means odd/strange and can sound negative.

records.nuance: 撮る means to take a photograph or film something. With 写真を, it means taking many photos; it does not imply video recording here.
records.logic: 写真を is the object being captured; たくさん indicates many photographs.
records.difference: 撮る is used for capturing photos/video; 写す（うつす） can also mean photograph, but has additional senses such as copying or depicting.

records.nuance: 再び means again or once more. Here he came back here again; 戻ってきた already means returned, so 再び emphasizes another return rather than a separate destination.
records.logic: It modifies the return as a repeated event; it does not say how long he had been away.
records.difference: 再び is somewhat formal; また（また） is a common conversational equivalent for “again.”

records.kanji_breakdown: 再 = again; 来 = come/next; 年 = year
records.nuance: 再来年 means the year after next, counted from the speaker’s time of speaking. The Olympics sentence uses that relative time expression; it does not specify a calendar year here.
records.logic: 再来年 is a set relative-time expression meaning the year after next; read the whole word conventionally rather than treating it as a literal etymology.
records.difference: 再来年 is two years ahead; 来年（らいねん） is next year.
records.filipino: sa taon pagkatapos ng susunod na taon

records.kanji_breakdown: チョーク = chalk; board-writing stick
records.nuance: チョーク is chalk, the stick used to write on a blackboard. The sentence says letters/characters were written with it; it does not specify the content.
records.logic: で marks the tool used to write, and 黒板に marks the surface.
records.difference: チョーク is chalk for a blackboard; マーカー is an ink marker used on a whiteboard.

records.kanji_breakdown: 再 = again; 来 = come/next; 月 = month
records.nuance: 再来月 means the month after next, counted from the speaker’s time of speaking. In this sentence, reservations are full up to that time; it does not state the calendar month.
records.logic: 再来月 is a set relative-time expression meaning the month after next; read the whole word conventionally rather than treating it as a literal etymology.
records.difference: 再来月 is two months ahead; 来月（らいげつ） is next month.
records.filipino: sa buwan pagkatapos ng susunod na buwan

records.kanji_breakdown:
再 = again
来 = come
週 = week
records.nuance: 再来週 means the week after next, counted from the speaker’s current week. 忙しい says the speaker will be busy then; no exact dates are given.
records.logic: This is a fixed relative-time word meaning two weeks ahead, not a calculation from today’s date.
records.difference: 再来週 is the week after next; 来週（らいしゅう） is next week.
records.filipino: sa linggo pagkatapos ng susunod na linggo

records.nuance: 放送 means broadcasting a program by radio or television. The sentence says that program will be broadcast next week; it does not specify the station or medium.
records.logic: The program is transmitted for public reception; 来週 sets the time.
records.difference: 放送 is broadcast transmission; 配信（はいしん） commonly means distributing content online/on demand.

records.nuance: 装置 is a device or piece of equipment arranged for a particular purpose. Here it is equipment used in an experiment; the sentence does not say what it does.
records.logic: The word points to a setup or apparatus serving a purpose; この marks the particular device.
records.difference: 装置 often suggests a purposeful apparatus or setup; 道具（どうぐ） is a more general tool.

records.kanji_breakdown: ティッシュ = facial tissue; tissue paper
records.nuance: ティッシュ commonly means a disposable paper tissue in everyday Japanese. The speaker asks for tissues to be passed; it does not mean biological tissue here.
records.logic: The surrounding request to pass it selects the household paper product.
records.difference: ティッシュ is a disposable paper tissue; ハンカチ is a reusable cloth handkerchief.

records.nuance: 仮名（かな） names the Japanese kana syllabaries (hiragana and katakana). In 仮名を振る, it means adding kana reading guides to a written name; the sentence asks for the name’s reading to be shown.
records.logic: The expression 仮名を振る is a conventional way to ask for kana readings to be attached; it is not asking for a temporary name.
records.difference: 仮名 means kana; 振り仮名（ふりがな） refers specifically to the reading guides added to text.
records.filipino: kana (mga karakter ng hiragana at katakana)

records.kanji_breakdown: 送 = send; 仮 = provisional; 名 = name
records.nuance: 送り仮名 is kana written after a kanji to clarify how a word is read, especially its inflection. The sentence says the okurigana is incorrect; it does not mean kana suffixes in general are wrong.
records.logic: In words such as 食べる, べる follows the kanji and is okurigana; the sentence refers to a particular spelling choice.
records.difference: 送り仮名 follows a kanji as part of its spelling; 振り仮名（ふりがな） is a reading guide attached to the kanji.
records.filipino: okurigana; kana na kasunod ng kanji

records.nuance: 鏡 is a mirror. Here she looks at herself in it and fixes her hair; the sentence does not say she is checking makeup.
records.logic: 鏡を見て is the means/context before she tidies her hair.
records.difference: 鏡 reflects an image; 窓（まど） is a window, which may also reflect but is not its primary function.

records.nuance: 悲しむ means to feel sorrow or grieve. Here the father is grieving his friend’s death; it describes his emotional response, not necessarily outward crying.
records.logic: 友だちの死を identifies the loss that causes the sorrow.
records.difference: 悲しむ describes feeling sorrow; 泣く（なく） means to cry, which may happen but is not stated.

records.kanji_breakdown: ノック = knock on a door
records.nuance: ノック means to knock, especially on a door to announce oneself or ask to enter. Here the request is to knock before going in.
records.logic: ドアを marks what is knocked on, and 入る時 indicates when to do it.
records.difference: ノック is the action of tapping on a door; 呼び鈴（よびりん） is a doorbell.

records.nuance: In 頭が固い, 固い is figurative: the boss is stubborn or inflexible in thinking. It does not describe the physical hardness of the head.
records.logic: The body-part phrase 頭が固い is an idiom for rigid thinking.
records.difference: 頭が固い means rigid-minded; 頑固（がんこ） is a common word for stubbornness more broadly.
records.filipino: matigas ang ulo; sarado ang isip

records.kanji_breakdown: 美 = beauty/art; 術 = art/skill; 館 = building
records.nuance: 美術館 is an art museum, a place that collects or displays works of art. The sentence only says the speaker went there yesterday.
records.logic: The compound denotes a museum focused on art; it is a type of museum institution.
records.difference: 美術館 focuses on art; 博物館（はくぶつかん） is the broader museum category for varied collections.

records.nuance: 美人 means a beautiful person and commonly refers to a beautiful woman. The sentence compliments his mother’s appearance; it does not specify personality.
records.logic: 美 modifies 人, describing appearance.
records.difference: 美人 is a person regarded as beautiful; 美しい（うつくしい） is the adjective “beautiful.”

records.kanji_breakdown: 美 = beauty; 容 = appearance; 院 = establishment
records.nuance: 美容院 is a hair/beauty salon. In this sentence, his father gets his hair cut there; it does not say the father works there.
records.logic: 美容院で marks the place where the hair service happens; Japanese omits the barber and does not require the subject to cut it himself.
records.difference: 美容院 is a salon for hair and beauty services; 理髪店（りはつてん） is a barbershop.

records.kanji_breakdown: よろしく = polite formula for a request or courtesy
records.nuance: よろしくお願いします is a conventional polite expression used when asking for cooperation, beginning a relationship, or closing a request. Its best English rendering depends on context; “my best regards” is only one possible paraphrase.
records.logic: よろしく expresses a wish for things to go well between the people; お願いします makes it a polite request.
records.meaning: please; thank you in advance; I look forward to working with you (context-dependent)
records.difference: よろしくお願いします is a set polite formula; お願いします alone means “please/I ask.”
records.filipino: magalang na pakikisuyo; salamat po sa pakikipagtulungan (depende sa konteksto)

records.kanji_breakdown: 博 = broad learning; 物 = things; 館 = building
records.nuance: 博物館 is a museum that collects, preserves, and displays materials. The sentence says the speaker visited a car museum, a specialized example; it does not mean a general art museum.
records.logic: A museum makes collections available for viewing, learning, or research; 車の specifies its subject.
records.difference: 博物館 is the broad museum term; 美術館（びじゅつかん） specializes in art.

records.nuance: 開催 means to hold or organize an event such as a meeting. In passive form, 開催された, the conference was held in Kyoto; the sentence does not name the organizer.
records.logic: The event is presented as taking place; passive grammar leaves the organizer unstated.
records.meaning: hold; hold an event; take place (passive)
records.difference: 開催 is used for meetings and events; 開会（かいかい） often means the opening/start of a meeting or session.

records.nuance: 特徴 is a noticeable characteristic or feature. The curves are presented as a distinguishing feature of the car; Japanese does not claim that no other car has them.
records.logic: It identifies a salient quality by which the car can be recognized.
records.difference: 特徴 is value-neutral and means a noticeable identifying feature; 特長（とくちょう） often emphasizes an advantage or strong point.

records.nuance: 許す has several senses, including permit and forgive. With 彼を and this sentence, it means the speaker forgave him; it does not mean permission was granted.
records.logic: The person marked by を is the one forgiven; the past form reports that the forgiveness happened.
records.difference: 許す means forgive here; 許可する（きょかする） specifically means permit or authorize.

records.kanji_breakdown: がらがら = nearly empty; sparsely occupied
records.nuance: For a movie theater, がらがら means nearly empty or with very few people. It is not the rattling sound sense of the same word.
records.logic: The theater is described as having little occupancy; the sentence does not state the exact number of people.
records.difference: がらがら is emphatic and suggests very few people; すいている（空いている） more neutrally means not crowded.

records.kanji_breakdown: 免 = exempt/release; 許 = permission; 証 = proof
records.nuance: 免許証 is an official document proving that a license has been granted. The request asks to show the credential; no particular kind of license is specified in this sentence.
records.logic: 証 marks a document that certifies 免許; the object of 見せる is the document itself.
records.difference: 免許証 is the proof document; 免許（めんきょ） is the license or permission itself.

records.nuance: 教師 is a teacher or instructor, especially someone who teaches in a school. 彼は高校教師だ says he is a high-school teacher.
records.logic: 高校 specifies the school level; 教師 names his teaching role.
records.difference: 教師 generally means a teacher/instructor; 教授（きょうじゅ） is commonly the academic title “professor.”

records.nuance: As a noun, 教授 means professor. The sentence identifies him as a chemistry professor; 教授 can also mean the act of teaching when used as a verbal noun, but that is not the sense here.
records.logic: 化学の identifies the academic field, and 彼は marks this as his position.
records.difference: 教授 as a noun is professor; 教師（きょうし） is the broader word for teacher/instructor.

records.nuance: 伝える means to convey or tell information to someone. Here the speaker asks that this matter be passed on to everyone; it does not specify how.
records.logic: みんなに marks the recipients and このこと the information to convey.
records.difference: 伝える is broad “convey/pass on”; 話す（はなす） means speak or talk.

records.kanji_breakdown: ぎらぎら = glare intensely; shine harshly
records.nuance: ぎらぎら describes a strong, glaring shine. With the sun as subject, it says the sun is shining fiercely/glareingly; it does not itself state the temperature.
records.logic: It emphasizes an intense brightness that catches the eye, rather than gentle sparkle.
records.difference: ぎらぎら suggests harsh, intense glare; きらきら more often suggests small, sparkling points of light.
records.filipino: matinding sikat ng araw; nakakasilaw na ningning

records.nuance: 鳥 is a bird. In this sentence, a bird is flying; it does not mean poultry or bird meat.
records.logic: The noun is the subject of 飛んでいます, describing the bird in flight.
records.difference: 鳥 refers to a living bird here; 鶏肉（とりにく） specifically means chicken meat.

records.nuance: 鳴る is an intransitive verb for a sound being produced. Here the telephone rang at five this morning; the sentence does not say who caused it.
records.logic: The thing that makes the sound is the subject; the telephone rings on its own in this sentence.
records.difference: 鳴る describes a sound occurring; 鳴く（なく） is used for animals making their characteristic calls.

records.nuance: 鳴く is used for animals making sounds. Here the cat is meowing somewhere; どこかで leaves its location unspecified.
records.logic: The animal is the subject that produces the call; the sentence does not identify the cat’s exact location.
records.meaning: call; make an animal sound; meow
records.difference: 鳴く is used for animal calls; 鳴る is used for a sound such as a phone or bell ringing.
records.filipino: umiyaw; gumawa ng tunog ang hayop

records.nuance: 声 means a voice. 大きな声で話した means he spoke in a loud voice; it describes volume, not anger.
records.logic: 大きな声 refers to the loudness of his voice, and で marks the manner of speaking.
records.difference: 声 is a voice; 音（おと） is the broader word for sound, including non-vocal sounds.

records.kanji_breakdown: そっち = that side; over there (informal)
records.nuance: そっち is an informal demonstrative for the listener’s side, that direction, or something there. Here it identifies the place as the speaker’s room; exact spatial distance depends on context.
records.logic: The demonstrative points to a place or side in the conversation; が identifies it as the room.
records.difference: そっち is casual; そちら（そちら） is a more polite form.

records.nuance: 卵 means an egg. The sentence says chickens lay eggs; it does not specify whether the eggs are intended for food.
records.logic: ニワトリ is the animal that lays 卵; the verb 産む means to lay or give birth.
records.difference: 卵 is an egg; 鶏肉（とりにく） is chicken meat.

records.nuance: 犬 means a dog. この犬 points to a particular dog described as clever; 賢い is about intelligence, not obedience.
records.logic: この identifies the dog being discussed, and とても賢い describes it as very clever.
records.difference: 犬 is a dog; 狼（おおかみ） is a wolf.

records.nuance: 馬 means a horse. Here he rode a horse at a ranch; the sentence does not say whether he rode for work or recreation.
records.logic: 馬に乗る is the ordinary expression for riding a horse; 牧場で gives the location.
records.difference: 馬 is the animal; 乗る（のる） means to get on or ride it.

records.kanji_breakdown: 駐 = stop; 車 = car; 場 = place
records.nuance: 駐車場 is a place for parking vehicles. The request is to leave the car in the parking area, not merely stop briefly on the road.
records.logic: The compound names a place where a car is left parked; に marks the destination/location.
records.difference: 駐車場 is a parking area; 車庫（しゃこ） is a garage or vehicle storage space.

records.kanji_breakdown: ピンポン = ping-pong; table tennis
records.nuance: ピンポン is a casual everyday term for table tennis. The sentence says the speaker played with a friend yesterday evening; 昨日の夕方 is evening and need not mean late at night, despite the deck’s “last night.”
records.logic: ピンポンをする is “play ping-pong”; 昨日の夕方 gives the time.
records.difference: ピンポン is casual; 卓球（たっきゅう） is the standard term, especially in formal or competitive contexts.

records.nuance: 騒ぐ means to make noise or behave noisily. Here it is a request not to make a racket on the train; it does not necessarily mean fighting.
records.logic: 電車の中で sets the place, and 騒がないでください politely asks someone not to behave noisily there.
records.meaning: make noise; make a racket; fuss
records.difference: 騒ぐ is noisy behavior; 話す（はなす） simply means to speak and can be quiet.

records.nuance: 刺す can mean prick, pierce, or sting. In the passive sentence, an insect stung or pricked the speaker on the arm; the insect type is unspecified.
records.logic: 虫に marks the cause/agent in the passive sentence, and 腕を marks the affected body part.
records.difference: 刺す is the action of piercing or stinging; 噛む（かむ） means to bite.
records.filipino: tusukin; tinuklaw ako ng insekto sa braso

records.nuance: 刺身 is a Japanese dish of thinly sliced raw fish or other seafood. The sentence says the speaker does not eat sashimi, without specifying a particular ingredient.
records.logic: 刺身 is the established name of a dish; the characters should not be treated as a literal description of how it is prepared.
records.meaning: sashimi; sliced raw fish or seafood
records.difference: 刺身 is served raw; 寿司（すし） may include vinegared rice and is not simply another word for sashimi.
records.filipino: sashimi; hilaw na isda o lamang-dagat na hiniwa

records.nuance: 激しい means intense or forceful. With rain, it means very heavy rain; the Japanese sentence does not specify a storm or damage.
records.logic: 激しい modifies 雨 and describes its intensity; 降っています says it is falling now.
records.difference: 激しい describes strong intensity; 強い（つよい） is broader and can mean strong without the same degree of forcefulness.

records.nuance: ぺこぺこ can describe being very hungry, repeatedly bowing, or something denting/rattling. With おなか, it means very hungry, not bowing.
records.logic: おなかがぺこぺこ is a set everyday expression for a very hungry stomach.
records.difference: ぺこぺこ is an emphatic colloquial way to say hungry; 空腹（くうふく） is the more neutral noun “hunger/empty stomach.”
records.filipino: gutóm na gutóm; gutóm na gutóm ako

records.nuance: 驚く means to be surprised or startled. Here he was surprised when he saw blood; the sentence does not say that he was afraid or fainted.
records.logic: 血を見て gives what he saw before the reaction; 驚いた is the past form of the intransitive verb.
records.difference: 驚く describes the reaction; 怖がる（こわがる） specifically means to be afraid.

records.nuance: 倒れる is intransitive: something falls or topples. Here the tree fell because of strong wind. The deck’s “gale” is a stronger English rendering than the Japanese 強風, which simply says strong wind.
records.logic: 木が is the subject that topples; 強風で gives the cause without naming an agent.
records.difference: 倒れる describes something falling; 倒す（たおす） means to make something fall.

records.nuance: 倒す is transitive and means to knock something down. Here the skier knocked over a pole; the sentence does not state why or where the pole stood.
records.logic: そのスキーヤー is the agent, and ポール is the object made to fall.
records.difference: 倒す is transitive; 倒れる（たおれる） describes the thing falling without an object causing it.

records.kanji_breakdown: 傾 = lean; incline; 向 = direction
records.nuance: 傾向 means a tendency or general pattern. The sentence presents a tendency among young people recently, not a claim that every young person avoids difficult books.
records.logic: 傾向がある marks a pattern that tends to occur; it does not state an absolute rule.
records.difference: 傾向 is a general pattern; 習慣（しゅうかん） is a habit repeated by a person or group.

records.nuance: ぺらぺら describes speaking a language fluently in this sentence. The word can also describe something thin/flimsy or rapid chatter in other contexts.
records.logic: ドイツ語がぺらぺらです is a colloquial description of her German fluency.
records.difference: ぺらぺら is casual and emphatic; 流暢（りゅうちょう） is a more formal word for fluency.

records.kanji_breakdown: 柔 = soft; gentle; 道 = way; path
records.nuance: 柔道 is judo, a Japanese martial art and sport. Here the speaker is learning/practicing it; the compound’s kanji are cues, not a literal definition of the sport’s techniques.
records.logic: 柔道 is the established name of the martial art; 習っています shows ongoing study or practice.
records.difference: 柔道 is a grappling martial art; 空手（からて） is a different martial art with its own techniques.
records.filipino: judo; isport na panlaban ng Hapon

records.nuance: 柔らかい means soft or pliable. Here it describes the futon’s physical feel, not a person’s gentle manner.
records.logic: 布団が marks the thing being described, and とても emphasizes its softness.
records.difference: 柔らかい is an i-adjective; 柔らか（やわらか） is the related na-adjective form.

records.nuance: 柔らか is a na-adjective meaning soft or gentle. With 声, it describes a gentle quality of his voice rather than a physically soft object.
records.logic: In 声は柔らかだ, the adjective describes the voice; the ending だ is the plain copula used with this na-adjective.
records.difference: 柔らか is a na-adjective; 柔らかい（やわらかい） is the closely related i-adjective form.

records.kanji_breakdown: 主 = main; principal; 張 = assert; stretch
records.nuance: 主張 is a point, position, or claim someone puts forward. Here the boss accepted the speaker’s position; “argument” in the deck English need not imply a quarrel.
records.logic: 私の主張 is the position being asserted, and 受け入れた says it was accepted.
records.difference: 主張 is a position put forward; 意見（いけん） is an opinion and can be stated less forcefully.

records.nuance: レインコート is a coat worn to keep rain off. The sentence says the speaker put one on because it was raining; it does not say whether an umbrella was also used.
records.logic: 雨なので gives the reason for putting on the raincoat; 着ました is the past of 着る for clothing.
records.difference: レインコート is worn on the body; 傘（かさ） is carried over the body to block rain.

records.kanji_breakdown: 引 = pull; draw; 張 = stretch; pull taut
records.nuance: 引っ張る is a transitive verb meaning to pull or tug. Here the daughter pulled her father’s hand; the Japanese does not specify how hard or in which direction.
records.logic: 私の手を is the object being pulled; 娘が marks the person doing the action.
records.difference: 引っ張る often suggests a sustained or forceful pull; 引く（ひく） is broader and can mean pull, draw, or lead.

records.kanji_breakdown:
突 = thrust; hit
当 = hit; meet
records.nuance: 突き当たる means to reach or run into an endpoint. Here the instruction is to turn right when you reach the end of the street; the Japanese does not specify a T-shaped junction.
records.logic: 突き当たったら means “when you reach the end”; 右に曲がる gives the action to take there.
records.difference: 突き当たる can mean physically reaching an endpoint; 行き詰まる（いきづまる） means becoming stuck in progress, usually figuratively.
records.filipino: dulo ng daan; pagdating sa dulo

records.kanji_breakdown:
突 = hit; reach
当 = meet; hit
records.nuance: 突き当たり is the end point reached by going straight. Here it says there is an endpoint ahead; the deck’s “T-intersection” is one possible layout, but that shape is not specified by the Japanese alone.
records.logic: The word names the endpoint at which forward travel stops; この先 places it ahead.
records.meaning: end point; end of a street; dead end
records.difference: 突き当たり identifies the endpoint; 行き止まり（いきどまり） explicitly describes a route with no way through.
records.filipino: dulo ng daan; hangganan ng daan

records.nuance: 壁 means a wall or partition. Here a picture is hanging on the wall; it does not identify the kind of room or building.
records.logic: 壁に marks the surface where the picture is hanging; 掛かっている describes its resulting state.
records.difference: 壁 is a wall in or around a structure; 塀（へい） is typically an outside wall or fence around property.

records.kanji_breakdown: アイス = ice cream; frozen dessert
records.nuance: アイス is a casual shortening used for ice cream or a frozen dessert. With 暑いので and 食べました, it means a cold treat, not solid water ice; the exact product is unspecified.
records.logic: The Japanese word is a casual shortening of アイスクリーム, and in this food context refers to a frozen dessert.
records.difference: アイス in this food context means a frozen treat; 氷（こおり） is water frozen into ice.

records.nuance: 弾く（ひく） means to play an instrument such as a guitar or piano. Here he plays guitar; it is read ひく, not はじく.
records.logic: The instrument is the object of 弾く; the exact reading is determined by the music context and the note’s Vocabulary-Kana field.
records.difference: 弾く（ひく） means play an instrument; 引く（ひく） means pull, draw, or lead, despite sharing the reading.

records.nuance: 丸い means round or circular. Here the earth is described as round; the sentence states its general shape without claiming a mathematically perfect sphere.
records.logic: 丸い describes the shape of 地球; it is a property of the subject.
records.difference: 丸い is an adjective; 丸（まる） is a noun for a circle or round mark.

records.nuance: 丸 can mean a circle or round mark. Here the speaker drew a large circle on paper; it does not mean a sphere.
records.logic: 丸 is the shape drawn, and 大きな describes its size.
records.difference: 丸 is commonly used for a drawn circle or mark; 円（えん） is the geometric term for a circle and is also the currency unit.

records.kanji_breakdown:
攻 = attack; assault
撃 = strike; hit
records.nuance: 攻撃 means an attack, including a military attack. The sentence says the United States attacked Iraq in 2003; it does not add a motive or describe the operation’s details.
records.logic: アメリカ is the actor, イラク the target, and 2003年に the time; 攻撃した reports the completed action.
records.difference: 攻撃 means attack; 防御（ぼうぎょ） means defense.

records.kanji_breakdown: いつごろ = about when; around what time
records.nuance: いつごろ asks approximately when. The speaker asks when the listener will take summer vacation; no exact date is requested.
records.logic: ごろ makes the time approximate, while いつ asks for the time period.
records.difference: いつごろ asks for an approximate time; いつ asks “when” without that explicit approximation.
records.filipino: mga bandang kailan; humigit-kumulang kung kailan

records.kanji_breakdown:
絶 = absolute; complete
対 = opposite; compare
records.nuance: 絶対に makes the refusal or prohibition emphatic: “absolutely not.” 駄目です can mean not allowed, unacceptable, or no good depending on context; the sentence gives no further reason.
records.logic: The adverb intensifies 駄目; it does not by itself say what consequence follows.
records.meaning: absolutely; definitely; under no circumstances (with a negative)
records.difference: 絶対に駄目 is a categorical “absolutely not”; 必ず（かならず） more often expresses certainty or something that must happen.

records.kanji_breakdown:
消 = extinguish
防 = prevent; defend
車 = vehicle
records.nuance: 消防車 is a fire engine/fire truck. The sentence says as many as four arrived; も adds emphasis or surprise about the number.
records.logic: 消防車 is the thing that arrived; 台 is the counter for vehicles, and も emphasizes the count.
records.difference: 消防車 is for firefighting; 救急車（きゅうきゅうしゃ） is an ambulance.

records.nuance: 嫌（いや） means disliked, unwanted, or unpleasant. Here the speaker dislikes waiting; “hate” in the English translation is stronger than necessary for every use of 嫌だ.
records.logic: 待つのが turns “waiting” into the thing the speaker finds unpleasant.
records.difference: 嫌（いや） describes something unwanted or unpleasant; 嫌い（きらい） is a noun/na-adjective meaning dislike or not liking.

records.kanji_breakdown:
大 = very; greatly
嫌 = dislike; detest
records.nuance: 大嫌い means to dislike or hate something very much. Here tests are strongly disliked; it is more emphatic than 嫌い.
records.logic: 大 intensifies 嫌い in this established compound; the sentence does not explain why the speaker dislikes tests.
records.difference: 大嫌い expresses very strong dislike; 嫌い（きらい） is less emphatic.
records.filipino: ayaw na ayaw; labis na kinaiinisan

records.nuance: ウィスキー is whisky. In このウィスキーは強いよ, 強い says it is strong; this may refer to its alcoholic strength or strong flavor, and the sentence does not clarify which.
records.logic: この identifies the whisky being discussed; 強い describes its perceived strength.
records.difference: ウィスキー and ウイスキー are spelling variants for the same drink; whisky’s strength may mean alcohol content or flavor.
records.filipino: whisky; inuming may alkohol na whisky

records.kanji_breakdown:
大 = most; large
抵 = reach; approximate
records.nuance: 大抵 means usually or in most cases. Here breakfast is usually eaten around seven; 大抵 does not mean every day without exception.
records.logic: 大抵 marks the usual pattern; 7時頃 gives an approximate time.
records.meaning: usually; generally; most of the time
records.difference: 大抵 means usually; 絶対に（ぜったいに） is emphatic and does not mean “usually.”

records.kanji_breakdown:
大 = many; large
勢 = group; force
records.nuance: 大勢（おおぜい） means many people or a large group. The sentence says they went out to eat in a group; the Japanese does not name who “we” are.
records.logic: 大勢で means doing something as a large group; the subject is omitted and supplied as “we” in the English translation.
records.difference: 大勢（おおぜい） is specifically many people; 多数（たすう） can refer to many things or people.

records.nuance: 姿 means someone’s visible figure or appearance. Here the speaker saw her figure in the distance; it says nothing about her personality.
records.logic: 遠くに gives the distant location, and 姿が見えた says her figure came into view.
records.difference: 姿 refers to a visible figure or appearance; 性格（せいかく） means personality.

records.kanji_breakdown:
姿 = form; appearance
勢 = posture; bearing
records.nuance: 姿勢 means posture or the way the body is held. Here the child’s physical posture is bad; it is not a comment on the child’s attitude.
records.logic: 姿勢が悪い is the ordinary expression for having poor posture.
records.difference: 姿勢 can mean physical posture; 態度（たいど） usually means attitude or manner toward something.

records.kanji_breakdown: エアメール = airmail; letter sent by air
records.nuance: エアメール means airmail, conventionally foreign mail carried by aircraft. The sentence does not name the destination, but the term itself commonly implies international mail.
records.logic: 彼に marks the recipient, and エアメールを送りました says the letter was sent by air mail.
records.difference: エアメール describes the delivery method; 普通郵便（ふつうゆうびん） is ordinary mail.
records.filipino: liham na ipinadala sa pamamagitan ng koreong panghimpapawid

records.nuance: 恐ろしい can mean frightening or terrible. With 夢, it means the speaker had a frightening dream; it does not establish that it was a premonition or a nightmare in a clinical sense.
records.logic: 恐ろしい modifies 夢; 昨夜 marks when the speaker had it.
records.difference: 恐ろしい often presents something as frightening or alarming; 怖い（こわい） commonly describes the person’s feeling of fear.

records.nuance: 怖い means scary or frightening. Here the speaker is afraid of dogs; the sentence expresses the speaker’s feeling, not a claim that all dogs are dangerous.
records.logic: 犬が怖い is a common pattern for saying one is afraid of dogs.
records.difference: 怖い describes fear; 恐ろしい（おそろしい） can describe something as objectively frightening or alarming.

records.nuance: 糸 means thread or yarn. Here the mother passed thread through the needle; it does not say what she was sewing.
records.logic: 糸を is the thread being passed, and 針に marks the needle it goes through.
records.difference: 糸 is thin sewing thread; 紐（ひも） is a cord or string, usually thicker and used for tying.

records.nuance: 孫 means grandchild. The sentence says a grandchild was born yesterday; Japanese leaves whose grandchild it is to context, while the English translation supplies “my.”
records.logic: 孫が生まれました reports a grandchild’s birth; the owner/relationship is not explicitly stated in this sentence.
records.difference: 孫 means grandchild; 子孫（しそん） means descendants or posterity.

records.kanji_breakdown: シャープペンシル = mechanical pencil; propelling pencil
records.nuance: シャープペンシル is a mechanical pencil with replaceable lead. In 私のシャープペンシルがありません, the speaker says theirs is missing; it does not mean a pencil sharpener.
records.logic: 私の marks the owner; がありません says the pencil is not present/available.
records.difference: シャープペンシル writes with replaceable lead; 鉛筆（えんぴつ） is a wooden pencil that is sharpened.

records.kanji_breakdown:
木 = tree; wood
綿 = cotton; fiber
records.nuance: 木綿（もめん） means cotton fiber or cotton cloth. In 木綿のシャツ it refers to the shirt’s cotton fabric, not a cotton plant.
records.logic: 木綿の modifies シャツ and identifies its material.
records.difference: 木綿（もめん） is cotton; 絹（きぬ） is silk.

records.nuance: 偉い can praise someone as admirable or important. Here it describes a scholar as distinguished; it does not necessarily mean morally kind.
records.logic: 偉い学者 describes the scholar as eminent or highly regarded.
records.difference: 偉い praises standing or achievement; すごい is a broad reaction meaning amazing or impressive.

records.nuance: 爪 means a nail on a finger or toe, and can also mean an animal’s claw. In this sentence the nails have grown; Japanese does not specify whose nails.
records.logic: 爪が伸びています says the nails have become longer and remain so.
records.difference: 爪 is the nail or claw itself; 指（ゆび） is the finger or toe.

records.nuance: 机 is a desk or table used for studying or working. Here the speaker says they were given a new desk; the Japanese leaves the giver implicit.
records.logic: 新しい机を買ってもらいました uses てもらう to say someone bought it for the speaker’s benefit.
records.difference: 机 is commonly a work or study desk; テーブル is a general table, often for meals.

records.kanji_breakdown: セロテープ = clear adhesive tape; cellophane tape
records.nuance: セロテープ is a common Japanese name for clear adhesive tape. Here the speaker asks whether any is available; “Scotch tape” is the deck’s English wording, not a required brand identification.
records.logic: セロテープはありますか asks whether the tape is present or available.
records.difference: セロテープ usually means clear office tape; ガムテープ is wider packing tape.
records.filipino: clear adhesive tape; teyp na pandikit

records.nuance: 棚 refers to a shelf or shelving unit. Here a large shelving unit is described as useful.
records.logic: 大きな棚 is the subject being evaluated as convenient or useful.
records.difference: 棚 is a shelf or shelving; 本棚 specifically means a bookcase.

records.kanji_breakdown:
本 = book
棚 = shelf; rack
records.nuance: 本棚 means a bookcase or bookshelf. The sentence comments on its size; it does not say what books it holds.
records.logic: 本 modifies 棚 to specify shelving for books; this is the established compound meaning.
records.difference: 本棚 is for books; 棚 is a general shelf or shelving unit.
records.filipino: aparador ng mga libro; estante ng libro

records.kanji_breakdown:
方 = direction; way
針 = needle
records.nuance: 方針 means a policy, plan, or guiding course. Here the future direction has been decided.
records.logic: The word refers to a guiding direction for action; the kanji are useful memory cues, not a literal etymological formula.
records.difference: 方針 is a guiding policy or course; 計画（けいかく） is a more specific plan.

records.kanji_breakdown: 釣 = fish; catch with a line
records.nuance: 釣る means to fish for or catch fish with a line. Here it means the speaker caught a large fish yesterday.
records.logic: 大きな魚を釣りました describes catching a fish by fishing; this verb is transitive.
records.difference: 釣る is catching fish with a line; 捕る（とる） is a broader verb for catching or taking animals.

records.nuance: やけど means a burn injury. 手にやけどをしました means he burned his hand; the sentence does not specify how.
records.logic: 手に marks the affected body part, and やけどをする means to get or suffer a burn.
records.difference: やけど is a burn injury; 傷（きず） is a wound or injury more generally.

records.kanji_breakdown: お釣り = change returned after payment
records.nuance: お釣り is the money returned after paying more than the price. Here the mother checked the change.
records.logic: お釣りを確かめた means she checked the amount returned to her after paying; お is a polite prefix.
records.difference: お釣り is change returned after payment; 小銭（こぜに） means coins or small change generally.

records.nuance: 鍵 can mean a key and, by extension, a lock. In 鍵を掛ける, the fixed expression means to lock up; the sentence does not specify a particular door.
records.logic: 鍵を掛ける is the standard expression “lock”; 出かける時 sets when to do it.
records.difference: 鍵 is the key or lock; 暗証番号（あんしょうばんごう） is a numeric passcode.

records.nuance: 鍋 is a cooking pot and can also refer to a hot-pot dish. Here soup is inside a pot; the sentence does not specify a particular dish.
records.logic: 鍋に marks the pot as the container holding soup.
records.difference: 鍋 is a pot or hot-pot meal; やかん is a kettle for heating water.

records.kanji_breakdown: 寿司 = conventional spelling of sushi; the kanji are not a literal ingredient breakdown
records.nuance: 寿司 means sushi, a Japanese dish commonly made with vinegared rice and toppings. Here she ate it for the first time; the kanji are conventional spelling and should not be read as a literal recipe.
records.logic: 寿司 is the established name of the dish; 初めて食べました says this was her first time eating it.
records.difference: 寿司 is the vinegared-rice dish; 刺身（さしみ） is sliced raw fish, usually served without sushi rice.

records.kanji_breakdown: アイスコーヒー = iced coffee
records.nuance: アイスコーヒー is coffee served cold, usually over ice. In this request, ください politely asks for one.
records.logic: アイス modifies コーヒー to identify the cold version; ください makes it an order/request.
records.difference: アイスコーヒー is cold coffee; ホットコーヒー is hot coffee.
records.filipino: kape na may yelo; malamig na kape

records.nuance: 泥棒 means a thief or burglar. 近所に泥棒が入った means a burglar broke into somewhere in the neighborhood; the English “burglary” describes the event.
records.logic: 泥棒が入った presents a thief entering or breaking in; it does not identify a specific house.
records.difference: 泥棒 is a person who steals or breaks in; 強盗（ごうとう） specifically means robbery, often involving force or threat.

records.nuance: 湯 means hot water, especially water prepared for bathing or drinking. お風呂のお湯 is bathwater; 一杯 here means full.
records.logic: お風呂のお湯 identifies the hot water in the bath, and が一杯 describes the bath as full.
records.difference: 湯 is hot water; 水（みず） is water without specifying that it is hot.

records.nuance: 沸く is intransitive: water boils, or a bath becomes heated and ready. Here the bath is ready, not literally boiling.
records.logic: お風呂が沸きました uses が with an intransitive verb: the bath water has heated up.
records.meaning: to boil; (bathwater) to be heated and ready
records.difference: 沸く describes something heating/boiling on its own; 沸かす is the transitive “heat or boil something.”
records.filipino: kumulo; uminit na ang tubig pampaligo

records.nuance: 沸かす is transitive: to heat or boil water. The request is to heat water, without specifying a particular appliance.
records.logic: お湯を marks the water being heated; 沸かしてください is a polite request.
records.difference: 沸かす means to heat/boil something; 沸く describes it becoming hot or boiling.

records.kanji_breakdown: あっち = over there; that way
records.nuance: あっち is an informal form of あちら, pointing to a place or direction away from both speaker and listener. Here it indicates the post office’s direction.
records.logic: 郵便局はあっちです locates the post office over there; it does not give a precise route.
records.difference: あっち is casual; あちら is the more polite form.

records.kanji_breakdown:
洗 = wash
濯 = rinse; wash
records.nuance: 洗濯機 is a washing machine. 新しい洗濯機を買いました says a new one was bought; Japanese omits the subject.
records.logic: 洗濯機 is the machine used for 洗濯, laundry/washing.
records.difference: 洗濯機 is the appliance; 洗濯 is the act of doing laundry.

records.kanji_breakdown:
洗 = wash
濯 = rinse; wash
records.nuance: 洗濯 means washing clothes or doing laundry. 一週間、洗濯をしていない means no laundry has been done for a week.
records.logic: 洗濯をする is “do the laundry”; していない indicates it has not been done.
records.difference: 洗濯 is laundry; 掃除（そうじ） is cleaning a room or space.

records.nuance: 濡れる is intransitive: the subject becomes wet. Here the speaker got wet because of the rain; しまった adds regret or an unwanted result.
records.logic: 雨で marks the cause, and 濡れてしまった describes ending up wet.
records.difference: 濡れる describes becoming wet; 濡らす is the transitive “make something wet.”

records.kanji_breakdown: あんなに = that; so much; to that extent
records.nuance: あんなに refers to something at that degree or in that way, often with surprise or emphasis. Here it emphasizes how exceptionally good a person can be.
records.logic: あんなにいい人 means “such a good person” or “a person that good”; the degree is the focus.
records.difference: あんなに points to a degree or manner associated with “that”; そんなに often refers to the listener’s situation or something already mentioned.

records.nuance: 怠ける means to be lazy or slack off. Here it is used in a negative command: stop slacking and help.
records.logic: 怠けていないで contrasts slacking off with the requested action 手伝って.
records.difference: 怠ける is slacking off; 休む（やすむ） is taking a rest and does not imply laziness.

records.kanji_breakdown: 一生懸命 = fixed expression: with all one’s effort
records.nuance: 一生懸命 means putting one’s full effort into something. Here it describes how he works every day; it emphasizes effort, not necessarily success.
records.logic: 一生懸命働いている modifies the manner of working: he works with sustained effort. Treat the compound as a set expression rather than a literal sum of kanji.
records.meaning: with all one’s effort; very hard; earnestly
records.difference: 一生懸命 emphasizes wholehearted effort; 熱心に（ねっしんに） means enthusiastically or diligently.

records.kanji_breakdown:
休 = rest
憩 = rest; repose
records.nuance: 休憩 means a break or rest period. 少し休憩しましょう is a suggestion to take a short break together.
records.logic: 休憩する means to take a break; しましょう makes it an inclusive suggestion.
records.difference: 休憩 is a break from activity; 休み（やすみ） is a broader rest, day off, or absence.

records.kanji_breakdown:
天 = sky; heaven
井 = well (memory cue)
records.nuance: 天井 means the ceiling inside a room or building. Here it is high; the sentence evaluates the room.
records.logic: 天井が高い describes the ceiling as high, literally “the room’s ceiling is high.”
records.difference: 天井 is an indoor ceiling; 屋根（やね） is a roof.

records.nuance: いたずら means mischief or a prank. Here the child loves playful tricks; it can also mean meddling or misbehavior depending on context.
records.logic: いたずらが大好き says the child likes mischief very much; it does not identify any specific prank.
records.difference: いたずら is a prank or mischief; 冗談（じょうだん） is a joke, which need not involve a trick.

records.nuance: 納豆 is natto, fermented soybeans with a distinctive sticky texture and strong smell. Here the speaker says they eat it often.
records.logic: 納豆をよく食べます states a frequent habit; the verb 食べる takes the food as its object.
records.difference: 納豆 is fermented soybeans; 豆腐（とうふ） is tofu, a different soy food.

records.kanji_breakdown:
化 = change; transform
粧 = adorn; dress (memory cue)
records.nuance: 化粧 means makeup or applying cosmetics. 化粧が上手い says she is skilled at makeup; it does not specify a particular style.
records.logic: 化粧が上手い describes her skill with makeup; 上手い evaluates ability.
records.difference: 化粧 is makeup/cosmetics; 化粧品（けしょうひん） means cosmetic products.

records.nuance: 畑 is a cultivated field, especially for crops other than rice. 畑仕事 means field or farm work; the sentence says the mother likes doing it.
records.logic: 畑仕事 is work done in a field; 好きだ expresses liking.
records.difference: 畑 usually refers to crop fields; 田（た） is a rice paddy.

records.nuance: 炊く means to cook rice or other food by boiling/steaming it in a pot or rice cooker. Here the mother cooks rice every morning.
records.logic: ご飯を炊く is the usual collocation for cooking rice; 炊く is transitive and ご飯 is its object.
records.difference: 炊く is commonly used for rice; 料理する（りょうりする） is the general “cook.”

records.nuance: ウェートレス is a loanword meaning waitress, a female restaurant server. It is less common in some modern settings that use gender-neutral staff terms. The sentence says the speaker called a waitress.
records.logic: ウェートレスを呼んだ means the server was called; the subject is omitted in Japanese.
records.difference: ウェートレス specifically refers to a woman; 店員（てんいん） is a gender-neutral employee or staff member.

records.nuance: 自炊 means preparing meals for oneself, often at home, rather than relying on restaurant or ready-made food. Here the speaker does it every day.
records.logic: 自炊している describes the continuing habit of cooking one’s own meals.
records.difference: 自炊 emphasizes making one’s own meals; 料理する is simply cooking and does not say for whom.

records.kanji_breakdown:
灰 = ash
皿 = dish; plate
records.nuance: 灰皿 is an ashtray. ください is a polite request for one; the sentence gives no further setting.
records.logic: 灰 (ashes) + 皿 (dish) describes the object’s function; it is a transparent modern compound, not a historical claim.
records.difference: 灰皿 is for cigarette ash; 皿（さら） is an ordinary plate or dish.

records.nuance: 灰 means ash or ashes left after something burns. Here everything became ashes in a fire.
records.logic: 灰になる means to turn into ash; すべて indicates everything.
records.difference: 灰 is ash; 煙（けむり） is smoke.

records.nuance: 灰色 means gray, literally the color of ash as a descriptive compound. Here it describes the sky today.
records.logic: 灰色だ is a noun-like color predicate describing the sky.
records.difference: 灰色 is gray; 白（しろ） is white.

records.kanji_breakdown: おばさん = aunt; middle-aged woman
records.nuance: おばさん can mean an aunt or, informally, a middle-aged woman. Here the family came to visit, so “aunt” is a plausible contextual reading, while the exact kinship is not explicit in this sentence.
records.logic: おばさん一家 means the woman’s family/household; 遊びに来ました means they came for a visit.
records.difference: おばさん is casual; 伯母（おば） / 叔母（おば） are written forms specifically meaning an aunt.

records.nuance: 西暦 is the Gregorian/Western calendar era used for ordinary year numbering in Japan. 西暦1964年 dates the event to 1964 CE.
records.logic: 西暦 marks the year using the common Western calendar, distinguishing it from Japanese era-year notation.
records.difference: 西暦 uses year numbers such as 1964; 元号（げんごう） dates years by Japanese era names.
records.filipino: taong Gregorian; taon sa karaniwang kalendaryo

records.nuance: 毛 means hair, fur, or fine body fibers. Here it is cat hair that got onto a sweater; 付いた means it stuck/adhered.
records.logic: 猫の毛 is cat hair/fur; セーターに marks where it stuck.
records.difference: 毛 can mean animal fur or body hair; 髪（かみ） specifically means head hair.

records.nuance: 髪 means the hair on one’s head. 髪を切りました means the speaker got a haircut; Japanese does not state who cut it.
records.logic: 髪を切る is “cut one’s hair”; in context it can mean having it cut by someone.
records.difference: 髪 is head hair; 毛 is hair/fur more generally.

records.nuance: 舌 is the tongue. 舌を出してください is a polite instruction to stick it out, often said during an examination, though the context does not specify why.
records.logic: 舌を出す means to stick out the tongue; ください makes it a request.
records.difference: 舌 is the organ in the mouth; 唇（くちびる） are the lips.

records.nuance: くし is a comb. Here it is the tool used to comb his hair; the sentence does not specify the comb’s material or type.
records.logic: くしで marks the tool, and 髪をとかす means to comb one’s hair.
records.difference: くし is used to arrange hair; ブラシ is a brush with bristles.

records.nuance: 臭い（くさい） is an i-adjective meaning smelly or stinky, usually with an unpleasant odor. Here the speaker says natto smells bad.
records.logic: 納豆は臭い assigns the adjective 臭い to natto; the subject is what gives off the odor.
records.difference: 臭い（くさい） usually implies an unpleasant smell; 匂い（におい） is a neutral noun for a smell or scent.

records.nuance: 匂い is a smell or scent; it can be pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral depending on context. いい匂い means a pleasant smell.
records.logic: いい匂いがする is the common expression “there is a pleasant smell” / “it smells good.”
records.difference: 匂い is neutral; 臭い（くさい） is an adjective that generally calls a smell unpleasant.

records.nuance: 居る（いる） means to be or stay somewhere for a person or animal. Here the speaker was at home all day; 居る is written with kanji, though いる is common.
records.logic: 家にいました marks being at home; 一日中 means throughout the whole day.
records.difference: 居る（いる） is used for people and animals; ある is used for objects and events.

records.nuance: 履く means to put on or wear footwear and other lower-body items such as trousers. Here she is wearing boots.
records.logic: ブーツを履いています describes the ongoing state of wearing boots; this verb is used for footwear.
records.difference: 履く is used for footwear/lower-body clothing; 着る（きる） is used for upper-body clothing.

records.kanji_breakdown: クリーニング = dry cleaning; laundry service
records.nuance: クリーニング commonly means professional cleaning, especially dry cleaning. The suit was sent to a cleaner; it does not mean the speaker personally cleaned it.
records.logic: スーツをクリーニングに出す is the standard expression for taking/sending a suit for professional cleaning.
records.difference: クリーニング is professional garment cleaning; 洗濯（せんたく） is washing clothes, often at home.

records.nuance: 戸 means a door, often a sliding or hinged panel, especially one separating rooms. Here the room’s door is open.
records.logic: 部屋の戸 identifies the room’s door; 開いています describes its open state.
records.difference: 戸 often suggests a panel/door; ドア commonly refers to a hinged Western-style door.

records.kanji_breakdown:
扇 = fan
風 = wind
機 = machine
records.nuance: 扇風機 is an electric fan that circulates air. Here, because it is hot, the speaker suggests turning it on.
records.logic: 扇風機をつける means to switch the fan on; つける is used for operating an appliance.
records.difference: 扇風機 circulates air with blades; エアコン cools/conditions the air.

records.nuance: 豚 means a pig. Here 豚は鼻が良い says pigs have a keen sense of smell; the sentence is a general statement, not about one particular pig.
records.logic: 鼻が良い literally says “has a good nose,” a common way to describe a keen sense of smell.
records.difference: 豚 is the animal; 豚肉（ぶたにく） is pork as food.

records.nuance: 豚肉 means pork, the meat of a pig. The sentence gives a simple opinion about its taste.
records.logic: 豚肉 is a compound naming meat from a pig; 美味しい describes it as tasty.
records.difference: 豚肉 is pork; 牛肉（ぎゅうにく） is beef.

records.kanji_breakdown: ごちそう = feast; special meal
records.nuance: ごちそう means a feast or special meal and can also mean a treat. Here dishes are laid out on the table; “delicious” in English is an interpretation, not a separate Japanese adjective.
records.logic: ごちそうが並んでいる says a special meal is arranged on the table; 上に marks its location.
records.difference: ごちそう is a special meal or feast; 食事（しょくじ） is a meal generally.

records.nuance: 鶏（にわとり） is a domestic chicken. This sentence says it crows each morning; Japanese 鶏 does not itself specify male, though English “rooster” does.
records.logic: その鶏は毎朝鳴きます describes the chicken’s recurring morning call.
records.difference: 鶏（にわとり） can mean a chicken of either sex; 雄鶏（おんどり） specifically means a rooster.

records.kanji_breakdown:
腕 = arm
時計 = clock; watch
records.nuance: 腕時計 is a watch worn on the wrist. 遅れている means it is running slow, not that the speaker is late.
records.logic: 腕時計 is a wristwatch; 遅れている describes the timepiece lagging behind the correct time.
records.difference: 腕時計 is worn on the wrist; 時計 can mean a clock or timepiece generally.

records.nuance: お菓子 means sweets, snacks, or confectionery. Here the speaker suggests giving some to everyone; the word does not specify a particular kind.
records.logic: みんなに marks the recipients, and お菓子をあげましょう proposes giving them snacks.
records.difference: お菓子 is snack/sweet food; 料理（りょうり） is prepared food or a dish.

records.kanji_breakdown: お辞儀 = a bow made by bending the upper body
records.nuance: お辞儀 means a bow made by bending the upper body as a greeting, thanks, or sign of respect. Here everyone bowed to the company president.
records.logic: 社長に marks the person they bowed to; お辞儀をする is the set expression “to bow.”
records.difference: お辞儀 is a bodily bow; 挨拶（あいさつ） is a greeting and need not include bowing.

records.kanji_breakdown:
ごちそう = feast
する = do (verb-forming)
records.nuance: ごちそうする means to treat someone to a meal or pay for their meal. Here the speaker offers to treat others to dinner tonight.
records.logic: 今日の夕食は私が identifies the dinner and the speaker as the one treating; ごちそうします is polite.
records.meaning: to treat someone to a meal
records.difference: ごちそうする means pay for/treat someone to a meal; 食べさせる means make or let someone eat.

records.kanji_breakdown: 寝坊 = oversleeping; getting up late
records.nuance: 寝坊 means oversleeping or getting up late. 今朝は寝坊しました says the speaker slept in this morning, without saying why.
records.logic: 寝坊する is the set expression for oversleeping; しました reports it happened this morning.
records.difference: 寝坊 is oversleeping; 寝過ごす（ねすごす） often means sleeping past a stop or intended time.
records.filipino: mahuli sa paggising; magising nang huli

records.nuance: 旗 is a flag or banner. Here it is moving in the wind; the sentence does not specify what it represents.
records.logic: 風に揺れている means it is swaying in the wind; 揺れる is intransitive.
records.difference: 旗 is a flag; 看板（かんばん） is a signboard.

records.kanji_breakdown:
鉛 = lead (metal)
筆 = brush; writing implement
records.nuance: 鉛筆 is a pencil with a graphite core, traditionally written using kanji that refer to lead and a writing brush. It is not made with metallic lead.
records.logic: 鉛筆を貸してください asks to borrow a pencil; を marks the item lent.
records.difference: 鉛筆 is a pencil sharpened as it is used; シャープペンシル is a mechanical pencil with replaceable lead.

records.kanji_breakdown:
万 = ten thousand (memory cue)
年 = year
筆 = writing implement
records.nuance: 万年筆 is a fountain pen, a reusable pen that writes with liquid ink. Here the speaker gave one as a present to their father.
records.logic: 父に marks the recipient, and 万年筆をプレゼントしました describes giving the pen as a gift.
records.difference: 万年筆 uses liquid ink; ボールペン uses a small rolling ball and paste/gel ink.
records.filipino: plumang fountain; panulat na may tinta

records.nuance: こぼれる means to spill, overflow, or fall out. With tears, it describes them spilling or streaming from the eyes; it does not necessarily imply crying loudly.
records.logic: 目から marks where the tears spilled from; 涙がこぼれた presents them as the thing that spilled.
records.difference: こぼれる is intransitive, “spill”; こぼす is transitive, “spill something.”

records.nuance: 箱 is a box or container. Here it is described as heavy; the sentence does not say what is inside.
records.logic: この箱 identifies this box, and 重い describes its weight.
records.difference: 箱 is a box with sides/lid; 袋（ふくろ） is a flexible bag or sack.

records.kanji_breakdown:
本 = book
箱 = box; container
records.nuance: 本箱 means a bookcase or book-storage cabinet. Here a magazine is put into it; despite 本 in the name, it can hold other reading material.
records.logic: 雑誌を本箱に入れました says the magazine was put into the bookcase.
records.difference: 本箱 is a storage case/bookcase; 本棚（ほんだな） is shelving for books.
records.filipino: aparador ng mga libro; lalagyan ng babasahin

records.kanji_breakdown:
手 = hand
袋 = bag; pouch
records.nuance: 手袋 are gloves worn on the hands. Here the speaker put them on because it was cold; Japanese uses the verb する for putting on gloves.
records.logic: 寒いので gives the reason, and 手袋をしました means wore gloves.
records.difference: 手袋 cover the hands; ミトン are mittens with fingers partly joined.

records.nuance: 袋 is a bag or sack, including a shopping bag. 袋はいりません politely says the speaker does not need one.
records.logic: 袋は marks the bag as the topic; いりません means it is unnecessary/not wanted.
records.difference: 袋 is a flexible bag; 箱（はこ） is a box or rigid container.

records.kanji_breakdown: こんなに = this; so much; to this extent
records.nuance: こんなに points to a degree or quality near the speaker, often expressing surprise. Here it emphasizes that the book is remarkably interesting.
records.logic: こんなに面白い means “this interesting”; the following 初めて signals this is an unprecedented experience.
records.difference: こんなに refers to this degree near the speaker; あんなに refers to a degree associated with something farther away or already known.

records.kanji_breakdown:
財 = wealth
布 = cloth; fabric
records.nuance: 財布 means a wallet or purse for carrying money and cards. Here the speaker left theirs at the office; Japanese does not specify whether it is a men’s wallet or purse.
records.logic: 会社に marks where it was forgotten; 財布を忘れた means the speaker left their wallet behind.
records.difference: 財布 is for money/cards; 小銭入れ（こぜにいれ） is specifically a coin purse.

records.kanji_breakdown:
毛 = hair; fiber
布 = cloth
records.nuance: 毛布 is a blanket, often a wool or fleece blanket. Here this blanket is described as warm; the word does not guarantee a particular fiber.
records.logic: 毛布は暖かい describes the blanket as warm.
records.difference: 毛布 is a blanket; 布団（ふとん） is bedding such as a Japanese futon/mattress or duvet.

records.kanji_breakdown:
布 = cloth
団 = group; mass (memory cue)
records.nuance: 布団 is Japanese bedding, commonly a padded mattress and/or quilt laid out for sleeping. Here the mother is airing bedding outside or in the sun.
records.logic: 布団を干している means she is airing the futon/bedding; 干す means to dry or air something.
records.difference: 布団 is bedding used for sleeping; 毛布（もうふ） is a blanket.
records.filipino: futon; kutson at kubrekama na inilalatag

records.kanji_breakdown:
小 = small
包 = wrap; package
records.nuance: 小包 is a parcel or package sent by mail. Here one arrived from a friend in France; the sentence does not say what it contains.
records.logic: フランスの友達から marks the sender/source, and 小包が届いた says the parcel arrived.
records.difference: 小包 is a mailed parcel; 荷物（にもつ） is luggage or a package more generally.

records.kanji_breakdown: ざあざあ = sound of heavy pouring rain
records.nuance: ざあざあ is a mimetic word for a loud, steady rush or downpour, often rain. Here it describes rain falling heavily.
records.logic: 雨がざあざあ降っている combines the sound/quality word with 降る, “rain falls.”
records.meaning: pouring heavily; in a steady rush
records.difference: ざあざあ suggests heavy rushing rain; しとしと describes gentle, steady drizzle.

records.nuance: 包む means to wrap or cover something. Here the speaker wrapped a present in attractive paper; で marks the material used.
records.logic: プレゼントを marks what is wrapped, and きれいな紙で the paper used.
records.difference: 包む means wrap/cover; 包装する（ほうそうする） is the more formal “package/wrap goods.”

records.nuance: 飾る means to decorate or display something. Here flowers were arranged on the table; it does not state whether they were in a vase.
records.logic: テーブルの上に marks where the flowers were placed/displayed; 花を飾る means decorate with flowers.
records.difference: 飾る means decorate/display; 置く（おく） simply means put/place.

records.kanji_breakdown:
手 = hand
帳 = ledger; notebook
records.nuance: 手帳 is a personal notebook, planner, or diary for schedules and notes. Here the speaker bought a new one; the exact type is not specified.
records.logic: 手帳 is the established word for a notebook kept at hand for personal records or plans.
records.difference: 手帳 is for personal notes/planning; ノート is a general notebook.

records.kanji_breakdown:
電話 = telephone
帳 = ledger; directory
records.nuance: 電話帳 is a telephone directory or phone book. The sentence asks someone to show it; it does not specify a printed or digital format.
records.logic: 電話帳を見せてください requests that the directory be shown.
records.difference: 電話帳 lists phone contacts/numbers; 住所録（じゅうしょろく） is an address book.
records.filipino: listahan ng mga numero ng telepono

records.nuance: ジャガイモ means potato. In this sentence it is an ingredient to buy for making potato salad; the loanword spelling is standard and no kanji breakdown is needed.
records.logic: ポテトサラダを作るから gives the reason, and ジャガイモを買ってきて asks someone to buy and bring potatoes.
records.difference: ジャガイモ is potato; サツマイモ is sweet potato.

records.nuance: 牛乳 is cow’s milk. The speaker says they drink it every morning; it does not specify whether it is hot or cold.
records.logic: 牛乳を飲む is the usual phrase for drinking milk; 毎朝 marks the daily time.
records.difference: 牛乳 is dairy milk; 豆乳（とうにゅう） is soy milk.

records.kanji_breakdown:
玄 = dark; mysterious (memory cue)
関 = barrier; checkpoint
records.nuance: 玄関 is the entry area of a Japanese home or building, where people enter and often remove shoes. Here flowers were decorated/placed there; the exact arrangement is not stated.
records.logic: 玄関に marks the entry area as the place where flowers were arranged.
records.difference: 玄関 is the entry area; 入口（いりぐち） simply means entrance/opening.

records.nuance: 眼鏡 means eyeglasses. 眼鏡をかけています says he is wearing them; the verb かける is used for glasses.
records.logic: 彼は眼鏡をかけています describes his current state of wearing glasses.
records.difference: 眼鏡 are corrective glasses; サングラス are sunglasses.

records.nuance: 眠い means sleepy or drowsy. Here the speaker feels very sleepy today; it describes a state, not that they are already asleep.
records.logic: 眠いです is an adjective describing the speaker’s current feeling.
records.difference: 眠い means feeling sleepy; 眠る（ねむる） means to sleep.

records.nuance: ソファ is a sofa or couch. 気持ちがいい means it feels pleasant or comfortable to sit/lie on; the sentence is about comfort.
records.logic: このソファは気持ちがいい describes the pleasant feeling of using the sofa.
records.difference: ソファ is upholstered seating for several people; 椅子（いす） is a chair.

records.nuance: 眠る means to sleep. Here the speaker slept for eight hours yesterday; the verb is intransitive.
records.logic: 8時間 marks the duration of sleep; 眠りました reports sleeping.
records.difference: 眠る is sleep; 寝る（ねる） can mean lie down or go to bed as well as sleep.

records.kanji_breakdown:
封 = seal; close
筒 = tube; cylinder (memory cue)
records.nuance: 封筒 is an envelope for letters or documents. Here the letter was put into it.
records.logic: その手紙を marks what was inserted, and 封筒に marks the envelope it went into.
records.difference: 封筒 holds a letter/document; 袋（ふくろ） is a general bag or pouch.

records.kanji_breakdown:
出 = go out
かける = set out (part of the verb)
records.nuance: 出かける means to go out or leave home for somewhere. Here 主人, the speaker’s husband in this context, has already gone out; the destination is unstated.
records.logic: もう出かけました means he has already left/set out. The subject and destination are understood from context.
