records.difference: 出かける means leave home to go somewhere; 出る（でる） means exit or come out more generally.
records.filipino: umalis; lumabas para pumunta sa kung saan

records.nuance: かかる has several meanings. With a clock and 壁に, it means to be hanging on the wall; here it is intransitive.
records.logic: 壁に marks the location, and 時計がかかっています describes the clock hanging there.
records.difference: かかる is intransitive (“be hanging”); 掛ける（かける） is transitive (“hang something”).

records.nuance: 煙草 means tobacco or cigarettes; its kanji spelling is conventional and should not be interpreted as a literal component definition. 煙草を吸う means to smoke.
records.logic: 彼は煙草を吸いません says he does not smoke tobacco/cigarettes; 吸う means smoke/inhale.
records.difference: 煙草 refers to tobacco/cigarettes; 葉巻（はまき） is a cigar.

records.kanji_breakdown:
掛 = multiplication (in this word)
算 = calculation
records.nuance: 掛け算 means multiplication. Here the younger brother is learning multiplication tables; “tables” is supplied by the English school-context translation.
records.logic: 掛け算を習っている means he is learning multiplication; 習う is to learn through instruction or practice.
records.difference: 掛け算 is multiplication; 足し算（たしざん） is addition.

records.kanji_breakdown:
拍 = beat; clap
手 = hand
records.nuance: 拍手 means clapping or applause. 大きな拍手が上がった says a loud round of applause arose; it does not identify who applauded.
records.logic: 拍手が上がった presents applause as beginning/breaking out; 大きな describes its volume or scale.
records.difference: 拍手 is applause; 歓声（かんせい） is a cheer or shout of excitement.

records.kanji_breakdown:
掃 = sweep; clean
除 = remove
records.nuance: 掃除 means cleaning or tidying a place. Here the speaker cleaned their room over the weekend; the word alone does not specify the method.
records.logic: 部屋の掃除をしました means “did the room cleaning”; 週末は marks when.
records.difference: 掃除 is cleaning generally; 掃く（はく） is specifically to sweep.

records.nuance: 掃く means to sweep with a broom or similar tool. Here the floor was swept with a broom; it is transitive.
records.logic: 床を marks the surface swept, and ほうきで marks the tool used.
records.difference: 掃く means sweep; 拭く（ふく） means wipe.

records.nuance: ちょうど means exactly or just the right amount or time. Here the price is exactly 30,000 yen, not an estimate.
records.logic: ちょうど modifies the amount to express an exact figure.
records.difference: ちょうど means exact/just; だいたい means approximately or roughly.

records.kanji_breakdown:
掃 = sweep; clean
除 = remove
機 = machine
records.nuance: 掃除機 is a vacuum cleaner. Here it broke; 壊れた is intransitive and does not state who caused it.
records.logic: 掃除機が壊れた says the vacuum cleaner broke; が marks the thing whose state changed.
records.difference: 掃除機 vacuums dust; ほうき is a broom used for sweeping.

records.nuance: 握る means to grasp, grip, or hold firmly. Here the girl took her mother’s hand; it can suggest a firm clasp.
records.logic: 母親の手を marks the hand she grasped; 少女は is the person doing it.
records.difference: 握る is grip/hold; 持つ（もつ） is hold or carry more generally.

records.kanji_breakdown:
握 = grasp; hold
手 = hand
records.nuance: 握手 means a handshake. 彼らは握手をした says they shook hands, a common greeting or sign of agreement.
records.logic: 握手をする is the set expression “shake hands.”
records.difference: 握手 is a handshake; お辞儀（おじぎ） is a bow.

records.nuance: 迎える means to meet, greet, welcome, or receive someone. Here the older sister will come to the airport to meet the speaker; 来てくれる adds that she kindly does so.
records.logic: 空港まで marks how far she comes, and 迎えに来る means come to meet or pick someone up.
records.difference: 迎える means go/come to meet or receive someone; 送る（おくる） means see someone off or send.

records.kanji_breakdown: ちょっと = a little; a bit
records.nuance: ちょっと means a little or a bit. もうちょっと means a little more; this is a casual request.
records.logic: もう modifies ちょっと to mean “a bit more,” and 塩を入れて asks for more salt to be added.
records.difference: ちょっと is casual; 少し（すこし） is a more neutral/polite “a little.”

records.kanji_breakdown: お巡りさん = police officer (familiar polite term)
records.nuance: お巡りさん is a familiar polite term for a police officer, often rendered “policeman” in older English. Here they suggest asking that officer for directions.
records.logic: あのお巡りさんに marks the officer as the person to ask; 道を聞く means ask for directions.
records.difference: お巡りさん is conversational; 警察官（けいさつかん） is the formal term for a police officer.

records.kanji_breakdown: いくつ = how many; how old
records.nuance: いくつ asks “how many?” and can ask someone’s age. With a daughter and になる, it means “how old has she become?”
records.logic: 娘さんはいくつになりましたか is a polite question about the daughter’s current age, not a count of objects.
records.difference: いくつ is a general count/age question; 何歳（なんさい） asks age more explicitly.

records.kanji_breakdown: 幾ら = how much; how many (established word meaning)
records.nuance: 幾ら asks “how much?” about an amount or price. Here the speaker asks the price of the shoes; the Japanese does not specify whether they mean one pair or multiple pairs.
records.logic: この靴は幾らですか asks the price of these shoes; 幾ら asks about an unknown amount or price.
records.difference: 幾ら asks for an amount or price; いくつ is more commonly used to ask how many items.

records.nuance: 冗談 means a joke or joking. 冗談は止めてください is a polite but firm request to stop joking.
records.logic: 止める means “stop,” and 冗談は marks joking as the activity to stop; ください makes the request polite.
records.difference: 冗談 is a joke; 嘘（うそ） is a lie and need not be humorous.

records.kanji_breakdown: つく = be on; light up
records.nuance: つく has several meanings. With a room light as subject, it means to be on or become lit; here the light is already on.
records.logic: 部屋の電気がついています describes the light’s resulting state; つく is intransitive.
records.difference: 電気がつく means a light comes on/is on; 電気をつける means turn a light on.

records.nuance: 穴 is a hole or opening. Here there is a hole in the sock; 開いている describes it as open/formed.
records.logic: 靴下に marks where the hole is, and 穴が開いている says a hole has opened.
records.difference: 穴 is a hole/opening; 傷（きず） is a cut or injury.

records.nuance: 寂しい means lonely, quiet, or emotionally desolate. Describing a song, it means the music feels sad or lonely; it does not say why.
records.logic: 寂しい曲 assigns a lonely or melancholy feeling to the song.
records.difference: 寂しい emphasizes loneliness or emptiness; 悲しい（かなしい） directly means sad.

records.kanji_breakdown: 丁寧 = careful; thorough; courteous (depending on context)
records.nuance: 丁寧 means careful, courteous, or thorough depending on context. Here it describes the careful way she works.
records.logic: 丁寧に modifies 仕事をします and describes the careful manner of working here.
records.difference: 丁寧 can mean careful/thorough or polite; 注意深い（ちゅういぶかい） specifically means attentive/careful.

records.kanji_breakdown: かわいそう = pitiful; deserving sympathy
records.nuance: かわいそう expresses pity or sympathy for someone in a difficult situation. Here the children lack food, which explains the speaker’s sympathy.
records.logic: かわいそうな modifies 子供たち; the next clause gives their hardship.
records.difference: かわいそう expresses pity for another; かわいい means cute/lovely.

records.kanji_breakdown: てんぷら = tempura; battered and fried food
records.nuance: てんぷら is food coated in a light batter and deep-fried, often vegetables or seafood. Here the speaker likes shrimp tempura; the kana spelling is used.
records.logic: えびのてんぷら identifies shrimp as the main ingredient/type of tempura.
records.difference: てんぷら is battered, deep-fried food; 唐揚げ（からあげ） is food coated and fried without a tempura batter.
records.filipino: tempura; pritong hipon na may balot na harina

records.kanji_breakdown: 怪我 = injury; getting injured (whole-word meaning)
records.nuance: 怪我 means an injury. Here she injured her arm; the sentence does not say how serious it was or how it happened.
records.logic: 腕を怪我した means she injured her arm; 怪我をする is the common expression for getting injured.
records.difference: 怪我 is an injury; 病気（びょうき） is an illness.

records.kanji_breakdown: 我慢 = endurance; putting up with something
records.nuance: 我慢 means enduring, putting up with, or restraining oneself. Here the speaker cannot tolerate his selfish behavior; the Japanese calls it わがまま.
records.logic: 彼のわがままには我慢できません means the speaker cannot put up with his selfish behavior; the phrase is a common whole-word usage.
records.meaning: to endure; put up with; restrain oneself
records.difference: 我慢 is enduring something unwanted; 忍耐（にんたい） is patience/endurance, often more formal.

records.kanji_breakdown:
幼 = young
稚 = young; immature
園 = garden; institution
records.nuance: 幼稚園 is a kindergarten or preschool for young children. Here the daughter attends one; 通う implies regularly going.
records.logic: 娘は幼稚園に通っています says the daughter regularly attends kindergarten.
records.difference: 幼稚園 is preschool/kindergarten; 保育園（ほいくえん） is a childcare center/daycare.
records.filipino: kindergarten; paaralan para sa maliliit na bata

records.nuance: 隠れる is intransitive: to hide or become hidden. Here the sun disappeared behind a cloud; it does not mean the sun intentionally hid.
records.logic: 太陽が雲に隠れた says the sun became hidden by a cloud; 雲に marks what obscured it.
records.difference: 隠れる is become hidden; 隠す（かくす） is transitive, hide something.

records.kanji_breakdown: とんとん = light repeated tapping
records.nuance: とんとん imitates a light, repeated tapping sound. Here the speaker tapped their mother’s shoulders; “as a massage” is added by the English translation, not explicit in Japanese.
records.logic: 肩をとんとんたたいた uses the sound word to describe the repeated light taps on the shoulders.
records.difference: とんとん suggests gentle, light taps; ぽんぽん can suggest quicker or more emphatic pats.

records.kanji_breakdown:
日 = sun; day
陰 = shade; shadow
records.nuance: 日陰 is a shaded place out of direct sunlight. Here, because it is hot, the speaker suggests resting in the shade.
records.logic: 日陰で休む means rest in a shaded place; で marks where the action happens.
records.difference: 日陰 is shade from sunlight; 影（かげ） is a shadow cast by an object.

records.nuance: 随分 means quite, very, or considerably, often with a sense that something is more than expected. Here the listener finished much earlier than expected.
records.logic: 随分早く modifies 早く終わった and emphasizes that the finish was considerably earlier than expected.
records.difference: 随分 often conveys “quite a lot/very” with surprise; とても is a more neutral “very.”

records.kanji_breakdown:
頑 = stubborn; firm (memory cue)
張 = stretch; hold firm
records.nuance: 頑張る means to do one’s best, persevere, or keep at something. Here it is an encouraging phrase for tomorrow’s exam.
records.logic: 明日の試験、頑張ってね encourages the listener to put in their best effort on the exam.
records.difference: 頑張る is an everyday encouragement/perseverance verb; 努力する（どりょくする） means make an effort more neutrally.

records.nuance: 頃（ころ） means around a time or period. 子供の頃 means during childhood; it does not identify an exact age.
records.logic: 子供の頃 sets the time for the repeated childhood activity described by よく遊んだ.
records.difference: 頃 is an approximate time/period; 時（とき） means time/when more generally.

records.kanji_breakdown: 人参 = carrot (established spelling; not a literal kanji breakdown)
records.nuance: 人参 means carrot. The kanji are an established spelling and should not be interpreted as a literal description of the vegetable. Here the speaker says they dislike carrots.
records.logic: 人参が嫌いだ states a general dislike of carrots.
records.difference: 人参 is carrot; 大根（だいこん） is daikon radish.

records.kanji_breakdown:
この = this
頃 = time; period
records.nuance: この頃 means these days, lately, or around this time. Here it refers to a recent recurring period in which the speaker often has stiff shoulders.
records.logic: この頃 sets a recent time frame for 肩が凝る; よく means often.
records.meaning: these days; lately; around this time
records.difference: この頃 points to these days/recently; 最近（さいきん） means recently more generally.

records.kanji_breakdown:
消 = extinguish
防 = prevent
署 = office; station
records.nuance: 消防署 is a fire station, the base for firefighters and fire response. The sentence says this town has only one.
records.logic: この町には消防署が1つしかありません uses しか〜ない to mean there is only one fire station in town.
records.difference: 消防署 is a fire station; 消防車（しょうぼうしゃ） is a fire engine.

records.nuance: 尋ねる has two main senses: ask/inquire or visit. With 道を, it means she asked for directions.
records.logic: 彼女は道を尋ねた means she asked about the way; 道を聞く is also common.
records.difference: 尋ねる means ask or visit depending on context; 聞く（きく） is the general verb “ask/hear.”

records.kanji_breakdown:
缶 = can; tin
詰 = pack; fill
records.nuance: 缶詰 means canned food, or food packed and sealed in a can. Here the fruit is canned and described as very sweet.
records.logic: 缶詰のフルーツ identifies fruit preserved in a can; 甘い describes its taste.
records.difference: 缶詰 is food sealed in a can; 瓶詰（びんづめ） is food preserved in a jar.

records.kanji_breakdown: ぬるい = lukewarm; not hot enough
records.nuance: ぬるい describes liquid or warmth that is lukewarm, cooler than desired. Here the bath was not warm enough; it does not necessarily mean cold.
records.logic: 風呂がぬるかった says the bathwater was lukewarm; ぬるい is a past-tense adjective.
records.difference: ぬるい is lukewarm/not hot enough; 熱い（あつい） is hot to the touch.

records.nuance: 缶 is a metal can or tin. Here it refers to the container holding the coffee; it does not say whether the coffee itself is hot or cold.
records.logic: その缶に marks the can as the container where the coffee is.
records.difference: 缶 is a metal can; 瓶（びん） is a bottle or jar.

records.nuance: 腐る means to rot or spoil, especially of food. Here the apple is rotten; the sentence does not specify how long it has been spoiled.
records.logic: リンゴが腐っている describes the apple’s spoiled state; 腐る is intransitive.
records.difference: 腐る is food going bad; 傷む（いたむ） can mean food deteriorates or gets damaged more broadly.

records.kanji_breakdown:
豆 = bean; soy
腐 = curd; ferment (word cue)
records.nuance: 豆腐 is tofu, a soft food made from coagulated soy milk. The sentence says the speaker eats it every day; it does not specify the type of tofu.
records.logic: 豆腐 is the established name of the food; the kanji are useful cues, not a literal description of how it is made.
records.difference: 豆腐 is tofu made from soy milk; 納豆（なっとう） is fermented whole soybeans.

records.nuance: 床（ゆか） means the floor of a room or building. Here it is wet; the exact cause is unstated.
records.logic: 床が濡れている describes the floor’s current wet state; 濡れる is intransitive.
records.difference: 床（ゆか） is a room’s floor; 地面（じめん） is the ground outdoors.

records.kanji_breakdown: パーセント = percent; per hundred
records.nuance: パーセント expresses a proportion out of one hundred. Here the Japanese says 80 percent of the village are elderly; the English supplies “people” to make the group explicit.
records.logic: この村の80パーセントは老人 means “80 percent of this village are elderly,” with residents understood from context.
records.difference: パーセント is a proportion per hundred; 割（わり） is another Japanese way to express a proportion, often per ten.

records.nuance: 床屋 is a barber shop. Here the sentence says hair was cut there yesterday; Japanese omits the person whose hair was cut, while the English translation interprets the subject as “I.”
records.logic: 床屋で marks where the haircut took place; 髪を切った means hair was cut.
records.difference: 床屋 is a barber shop; 美容院（びよういん） is a hair salon.

records.nuance: 畳（たたみ） is a traditional Japanese floor mat. 畳の部屋 is a room with tatami flooring; it does not specify how many mats.
records.logic: 畳の部屋 identifies the room by its tatami floor.
records.difference: 畳 is a tatami mat; カーペット is carpet.

records.nuance: 畳む means to fold or fold up. With 布団, it means to fold/store the bedding after use.
records.logic: 布団を畳んでください asks the listener to fold the futon; を marks the item acted on.
records.difference: 畳む means fold something up; 敷く（しく） means lay or spread it flat.

records.nuance: 干す means hang or spread something out to dry, often laundry in the sun or air. Here the mother is hanging out the laundry.
records.logic: 洗濯物を干しています describes the ongoing action of drying laundry; 干す is transitive.
records.meaning: to hang out to dry; dry
records.difference: 干す is dry by hanging/exposing to air or sun; 乾かす（かわかす） is the general transitive “dry.”

records.nuance: ひざ means the knee. Here the speaker injured their knee while skiing; the kana spelling is used.
records.logic: スキーで marks the activity/circumstance, and ひざを怪我しました says the knee was injured.
records.difference: ひざ is the knee; ひじ is the elbow.

records.nuance: 帽子 means a hat or cap. Because it is hot, the speaker suggests wearing one; 被る is the verb used for putting a hat on the head.
records.logic: 暑いので gives the reason, and 帽子を被りましょう proposes wearing a hat.
records.difference: 帽子 is headwear; ヘルメット is a protective helmet.

records.kanji_breakdown: ぜひ = by all means; definitely
records.nuance: ぜひ expresses a strong wish or recommendation that something happen. Here it makes the invitation warm and earnest: please do come to my home.
records.logic: ぜひ modifies 来てください, emphasizing the speaker’s sincere invitation.
records.meaning: by all means; definitely; please do
records.difference: ぜひ conveys an earnest wish; 必ず（かならず） more directly means certainly/without fail.
records.filipino: huwag mag-atubiling pumunta; malugod kayong inaanyayahan

records.kanji_breakdown:
敬 = respect
語 = language; word
records.nuance: 敬語 is honorific/polite language used to show respect or manage social relationships. Here the instruction is to use it with customers.
records.logic: お客様には marks the people addressed; 敬語を使いなさい instructs the listener to use respectful language.
records.difference: 敬語 is a language system showing respect; 丁寧語（ていねいご） is the polite-form subset of it.
records.filipino: magalang na pananalita; pananalitang nagpapakita ng paggalang

records.kanji_breakdown:
尊 = esteem; honor
敬 = respect
records.nuance: 尊敬 means respect or admiration for someone. Here the grandfather is respected by the whole family; the Japanese uses passive voice.
records.logic: 家族みんなに尊敬されています means “is respected by everyone in the family”; に marks who gives the respect.
records.difference: 尊敬 is respect/admiration; 尊重（そんちょう） is valuing or respecting a person’s rights, views, or choices.

records.nuance: ひじ means the elbow. The sentence says he injured it; the kana spelling is used.
records.logic: ひじに怪我をした marks the elbow as the injured body part.
records.difference: ひじ is the elbow; ひざ is the knee.

records.nuance: 敷く means spread or lay something flat over a surface. Here the speaker laid out a futon for the first time ever.
records.logic: 布団を敷いた means the futon was laid out; 生まれて初めて means “for the first time in one’s life.”
records.difference: 敷く means lay/spread something on a surface; 畳む（たたむ） means fold it up.

records.nuance: 雷（かみなり） refers to thunder and lightning as a storm phenomenon. 雷が鳴っています specifically says thunder is rumbling; it does not state whether lightning is visible.
records.logic: 雷が鳴る is the expression for thunder sounding; ています describes it happening now.
records.difference: 雷 can refer to thunder/lightning; 稲妻（いなずま） specifically means a flash of lightning.

records.nuance: 零（れい） means zero. In 零時 it denotes zero o’clock, or midnight; 今ちょうど emphasizes the exact time.
records.logic: 零時 is midnight (00:00); ちょうど means exactly.
records.difference: 零時 is midnight; 正午（しょうご） is noon.

records.kanji_breakdown: 仕舞う = put away; store (whole-word meaning)
records.nuance: 仕舞う means put something away or store it. Here she put important documents away in her desk; it can also mean finish doing something in other constructions.
records.logic: 書類を机に仕舞った means the documents were put away in the desk; 机に marks the destination.
records.difference: 仕舞う means put away/store; 片付ける（かたづける） means tidy up or put things in order.

records.nuance: ひも is a string or cord. Here it is a shoelace, and 切れた says it snapped/broke; kana is used.
records.logic: 靴のひも identifies the shoe’s lace; が切れた means it broke.
records.difference: ひも is a cord/string; ロープ is a thicker rope.

records.nuance: 踊る means to dance. Here she likes dancing at a club; のが好き expresses liking the activity.
records.logic: クラブで marks where she dances, and 踊るのが好きです means she likes to dance.
records.difference: 踊る is dance; 舞う（まう） often suggests graceful or formal dancing/movement.

records.nuance: 踊り is a dance or dancing style. Here the dance is described as easy to do/learn; 易しい means easy.
records.logic: この踊りは易しい describes the dance itself as easy; よ is explanatory emphasis.
records.difference: 踊り is a dance/dance style; 踊る（おどる） is the verb “to dance.”

records.nuance: 踏む means step on, tread on, or press with the foot. Here the driver pressed the brake pedal.
records.logic: ブレーキを踏んだ uses を for the brake being pressed; the subject is the driver.
records.meaning: to step on; tread; press with the foot
records.difference: 踏む means press/step on with the foot; 押す（おす） is a general “push.”

records.kanji_breakdown:
踏 = step; tread
切 = cut; cross (word cue)
records.nuance: 踏切 is a railway level crossing where a road crosses train tracks. The sentence says that crossing is long; it does not explicitly mention a signal or waiting time.
records.logic: その踏切は長い describes the crossing’s length; the English “signal” adds an object not stated in Japanese.
records.difference: 踏切 is the rail crossing; 横断歩道（おうだんほどう） is a pedestrian crosswalk.

records.nuance: まく has several meanings/readings depending on kanji and context. With beans in a February event, it means scatter or throw beans; the exact reading here is まく.
records.logic: 豆をまく means scatter beans; the event is described as taking place in February, without naming it in the sentence.
records.difference: まく（撒く） means scatter/sow; 投げる（なげる） is the general verb “throw.”

records.nuance: 蹴る means kick with the foot. Here the goalkeeper kicked the ball; it is a transitive verb.
records.logic: ボールを marks the ball kicked, and ゴールキーパーが marks who kicked it.
records.difference: 蹴る is kick with the foot; 打つ（うつ） means hit/strike more generally.

records.kanji_breakdown:
食 = eat; food
堂 = hall; building
records.nuance: 食堂 is a dining hall or cafeteria. Here it is the university cafeteria, described as inexpensive.
records.logic: 大学の食堂 identifies the university dining hall; 安い describes its price level.
records.difference: 食堂 is a place to eat, often a cafeteria; レストラン is a restaurant.

records.nuance: 猫 means cat. The speaker loves cats; 大好き expresses strong liking.
records.logic: 猫が大好きです means cats are the thing the speaker likes very much.
records.difference: 猫 is a cat; 犬（いぬ） is a dog.

records.kanji_breakdown:
文 = sentence; writing
章 = section; passage
records.nuance: 文章 means a piece of writing or a written passage. Here it says he writes very well; it does not necessarily mean handwriting is neat.
records.logic: 文章がうまい evaluates his writing or composition as skillful.
records.difference: 文章 is a written text/composition; 字（じ） means a character or handwriting.

records.nuance: やかん is a kettle used for heating water. Here water was boiled in it; the Japanese sentence omits who did it, while the English says “I.”
records.logic: やかんで marks the kettle used, and お湯を沸かしました says hot water was boiled.
records.difference: やかん is a kettle for heating water; 鍋（なべ） is a cooking pot.

records.kanji_breakdown: 丈夫 = sturdy; robust; healthy (whole-word meaning)
records.nuance: 丈夫 describes something strong or durable, or a person physically robust/healthy. Here it describes the grandmother’s body/constitution.
records.logic: 身体が丈夫だ means to have a strong, healthy body; 身体が is the quality being described.
records.difference: 丈夫 describes physical robustness; 元気（げんき） means energetic or well more generally.

records.nuance: また means again or also, depending on context. With 来ます tomorrow, it means the speaker will come again.
records.logic: 明日、また来ます means “I’ll come again tomorrow”; the destination is understood from context.
records.difference: また means again/also; もう一度（もういちど） more explicitly means one more time.

records.kanji_breakdown:
お = polite/respectful prefix
祖父 = grandfather
records.nuance: お祖父さん is a respectful term for someone’s grandfather. Here it is the speaker’s grandfather, who takes a walk every day.
records.logic: 私のお祖父さん identifies the speaker’s grandfather; 毎日散歩します describes his daily habit.
records.difference: お祖父さん is respectful/conversational; 祖父（そふ） is the neutral term for one’s own grandfather when speaking to others.

records.kanji_breakdown:
お = polite/respectful prefix
祖母 = grandmother
records.nuance: お祖母さん is a respectful term for someone’s grandmother. Here she lives with the woman; the Japanese does not specify whose grandmother she is.
records.logic: 彼女はお祖母さんと住んでいる says she lives with her grandmother; と marks the person she lives with.
records.difference: お祖母さん is respectful/conversational; 祖母（そぼ） is the neutral term for one’s own grandmother when speaking to others.

records.nuance: ようこそ is a welcoming expression used when someone arrives or enters. 日本へようこそ welcomes someone to Japan.
records.logic: 日本へ marks the place the visitor has arrived at; ようこそ is the welcome itself.
records.difference: ようこそ welcomes someone on arrival; いらっしゃいませ is the standard greeting to customers.

records.nuance: 祖父（そふ） means grandfather, usually one’s own grandfather when speaking about him to others. Here he is well; the Japanese omits “my.”
records.logic: 祖父は元気です says the grandfather is well; Japanese leaves the possessor implicit.
records.difference: 祖父（そふ） is one’s grandfather; お祖父さん（おじいさん） is a respectful/conversational form.

records.nuance: 祖母（そぼ） means grandmother, usually one’s own grandmother when speaking about her to others. Here she was born in Kyoto; Japanese omits “my.”
records.logic: 祖母は京都で生まれました says the grandmother was born in Kyoto; the English supplies the possessor.
records.difference: 祖母（そぼ） is one’s grandmother; お祖母さん（おばあさん） is a respectful/conversational form.

records.kanji_breakdown: 邪魔 = obstacle; in the way (whole-word meaning)
records.nuance: 邪魔 means an obstruction or being in someone’s way. Here it is a blunt request to move; tone may sound rude without softening.
records.logic: 邪魔です、どいてください means “You’re in the way; please move”; どいて is a direct request.
records.meaning: obstruction; in the way; to hinder
records.difference: 邪魔 means obstructing/being in the way; 迷惑（めいわく） means causing trouble or inconvenience.

records.nuance: 風邪薬 is medicine for a common cold, such as cold-relief medicine. この風邪薬を飲みなさい instructs someone to take this medicine.
records.logic: 風邪薬 is the established compound for cold medicine; を marks it as what should be taken.
records.difference: 風邪薬 treats cold symptoms; 薬（くすり） is medicine generally.

records.kanji_breakdown: ウェーター = waiter; male server
records.nuance: ウェーター is a loanword for a male waiter/server. In current usage, gender-neutral terms such as スタッフ may be preferred in some settings. Here the waiter brought water.
records.logic: ウェーターが marks the server who brought water; 運んできました means brought it over.
records.difference: ウェーター specifically indicates a man; 店員（てんいん） is a gender-neutral employee/server.

records.kanji_breakdown:
風呂 = bath
屋 = shop; place
records.nuance: 風呂屋 is a public bathhouse, especially a neighborhood bath facility. The sentence says the speaker went with a friend; Japanese uses the polite お風呂屋さん.
records.logic: 友達と marks the companion, and お風呂屋さんに行った means they went to a public bath.
records.difference: 風呂屋 is a public bathhouse; 家の風呂 is a bath at home.

records.nuance: 風呂 means a bath or bathtub; お風呂に入る is the usual expression for taking a bath. Here the father is bathing now.
records.logic: お風呂に入っています literally says he is in the bath; it commonly means he is taking a bath.
records.difference: 風呂 is a bath/bathtub; シャワー is a shower.

records.nuance: 昭和 is the name of a Japanese imperial era, 1926–1989. 昭和生まれ means born during that era; the sentence does not give exact birth years.
records.logic: 昭和生まれ identifies the era in which the parents were born.
records.difference: 昭和 is the era name; 平成（へいせい） is the following era.

records.nuance: 紫 is the color purple or violet. Here it describes the dress she wore; the sentence is in the past.
records.logic: 紫のドレス means a purple dress; の connects the color to the clothing.
records.difference: 紫 is purple/violet; 青（あお） is blue.

records.kanji_breakdown: そんなに = that much; to that degree
records.nuance: そんなに refers to a degree or amount already indicated or associated with the listener/context. In a negative sentence, it means “that much” is beyond what can be done.
records.logic: 一度にそんなにたくさんはできない means one cannot do that many things/that much all at once.
records.difference: そんなに points to a degree/amount in context; こんなに points to one close to the speaker or being directly shown.

records.kanji_breakdown:
紅 = deep red (word cue)
茶 = tea
records.nuance: 紅茶 means black tea in English: fully oxidized tea that Japanese names “red tea” by the leaf/liquor color. Here the speaker wants warm/hot black tea.
records.logic: 温かい modifies 紅茶, and 飲みたい expresses the speaker’s desire to drink it.
records.difference: 紅茶 is black tea; 緑茶（りょくちゃ） is green tea.

records.kanji_breakdown: 梅雨 = rainy season (whole-word meaning; spelling does not mean the rain is about plums)
records.nuance: 梅雨 is Japan’s early-summer rainy season. 梅雨は6月頃 says it is around June; timing varies by region and year.
records.logic: 6月頃 gives an approximate month, and 頃 means around that time.
records.difference: 梅雨 is the seasonal rainy period; 雨季（うき） is rainy season more generally.

records.nuance: 桃 is a peach, the fruit. 私の一番好きな果物 means it is the speaker’s favorite fruit.
records.logic: 桃です identifies the favorite fruit; 一番好き means liked most.
records.difference: 桃 is a peach; 梨（なし） is a pear.

records.nuance: 遭う（あう） means encounter or suffer an unwelcome event, such as an accident. Here it means he was involved in a traffic accident, not that he deliberately met one.
records.logic: 交通事故に遭った is the set expression for being involved in/meeting with a traffic accident.
records.difference: 遭う is used for unwelcome events; 会う（あう） means meet a person.

records.nuance: 枕 is a pillow. 低い means low in height; the English “thin” is an approximate translation, but the Japanese specifically says the speaker likes a low pillow.
records.logic: 低い枕 describes the pillow’s height, not necessarily its thickness.
records.difference: 枕 supports the head during sleep; クッション is a cushion for seating or support.

records.nuance: 嘘 means a lie or false statement. 嘘をつく is the common verb phrase “to lie”; the sentence warns against doing so.
records.logic: 嘘をついてはいけません means “must not tell a lie”; てはいけない expresses prohibition.
records.difference: 嘘 is a lie; 間違い（まちがい） is a mistake and need not be intentional.

records.kanji_breakdown: 遠慮 = reserve; politely holding back or declining (whole-word meaning)
records.nuance: 遠慮 means restraint, reserve, or politely holding back. In this reply, 私は遠慮します is a tactful way to decline an offer; it does not mean physical distance.
records.logic: 遠慮します is a conventional polite refusal, often used instead of a direct “no.”
records.difference: 遠慮する is hold back/decline politely; 断る（ことわる） means refuse more directly.

records.nuance: 叱る means scold or reprimand someone, often a child or subordinate. Here a father is scolding a child/children; Japanese does not specify “his” or the number.
records.logic: 父親が子供を叱っている identifies a father scolding a child; を marks who is being scolded.
records.difference: 叱る is scold/reprimand; 怒る（おこる） means get angry or scold, depending on context.

records.nuance: 傘 is an umbrella. 電車に傘を忘れた means an umbrella was left on the train; the Japanese omits the subject, while English supplies “I.”
records.logic: 電車に marks where the umbrella was left; 忘れる means forget/leave behind.
records.difference: 傘 protects from rain; 日傘（ひがさ） is a parasol used for sun.

records.kanji_breakdown: おじょうさん = young lady; someone’s daughter
records.nuance: おじょうさん is a respectful way to refer to someone else’s daughter or a young lady. Here it is a polite question about her age; exact relationship depends on context.
records.logic: おじょうさんはおいくつですか politely asks how old the young lady/daughter is.
records.difference: おじょうさん is respectful; 娘さん（むすめさん） is another polite term for someone’s daughter.
records.filipino: dalaga; anak na babae (magalang na tawag)

records.kanji_breakdown:
年 = year
賀 = congratulations
状 = card; letter
records.nuance: 年賀状 is a New Year greeting card, traditionally sent to arrive around New Year. Here one was sent yesterday; the date of arrival is not stated.
records.logic: 年賀状を出す means send a New Year card; 出す refers to sending/mailing it.
records.difference: 年賀状 is specifically a New Year’s greeting card; はがき is a postcard generally.

records.nuance: 賑やか describes a lively, bustling place with activity or people. Here Asakusa is described as a lively town; it need not mean noisy in a negative way.
records.logic: 賑やかな街 uses the adjective to describe the town.
records.difference: 賑やか describes lively activity; 静か（しずか） means quiet.

records.nuance: 蚊 is a mosquito. 蚊に足を刺された says a mosquito bit/stung the speaker on the leg/foot; Japanese does not specify the English possessive “my.”
records.logic: 蚊に marks the biter, 足を the body part, and 刺された is passive “was bitten/stung.”
records.difference: 蚊 is a mosquito; ハエ is a fly.

records.nuance: 拭く means wipe or rub a surface dry with a cloth/towel. Here the speaker wiped their body with a towel; the English “dried myself” is a natural interpretation.
records.logic: タオルで体を拭きました marks the towel as tool and body as the thing wiped.
records.difference: 拭く means wipe with a cloth; 洗う（あらう） means wash with water.
records.filipino: punasan; patuyuin sa pamamagitan ng pagpupunas

records.nuance: 挨拶 means a greeting or polite acknowledgment. Here she greeted someone with a smile; the Japanese does not state “me” as the recipient.
records.logic: 笑顔で marks the manner, and 挨拶した says she greeted someone.
records.difference: 挨拶 is a greeting/acknowledgment; 自己紹介（じこしょうかい） is a self-introduction.

records.nuance: 伴う means accompany or be associated with something, often as a consequence. Here the job entails danger; it does not say an accident has happened.
records.logic: その仕事は危険を伴う says danger accompanies/is inherent in the work.
records.meaning: to accompany; entail; be associated with
records.difference: 伴う means accompany/entail; 含む（ふくむ） means contain/include.

records.nuance: 巻く means wrap, wind, or roll something around an object. Here a towel was wrapped around his head; Japanese does not specify that it was tied.
records.logic: 頭にタオルを巻いていた means he had a towel wrapped around his head.
records.difference: 巻く means wrap/wind around; 結ぶ（むすぶ） means tie/knot.

records.nuance: 靴 means shoes or footwear. Here the shoes got dirty; Japanese leaves whose shoes they are unstated, despite “my” in English.
records.logic: 靴が汚れた describes the shoes becoming dirty; 汚れる is intransitive.
records.difference: 靴 is footwear; 靴下（くつした） means socks.

records.kanji_breakdown:
靴 = shoe
下 = below; under
records.nuance: 靴下 means socks. この靴下は3足で1000円 indicates the item is sold as three pairs for 1,000 yen.
records.logic: 3足 is three pairs; で marks the price for that quantity.
records.difference: 靴下 are socks; ストッキング are thin hosiery/stockings.

records.nuance: 磨く means polish, brush, or scrub until clean/shiny. With shoes, it means polish them.
records.logic: 靴を磨いてください asks the listener to polish the shoes; を marks what is polished.
records.difference: 磨く means polish/brush; 洗う means wash.

records.kanji_breakdown:
歯 = tooth
磨 = brush; polish
records.nuance: 歯磨き means brushing one’s teeth and can also refer to toothpaste. In this question it asks whether the person has brushed their teeth.
records.logic: 歯磨きをする is the usual phrase for brush one’s teeth; はしましたか asks if it has been done.
records.difference: 歯磨き can mean the act of brushing or toothpaste; 歯ブラシ is a toothbrush.

records.kanji_breakdown:
廊 = corridor
下 = under; passage (word cue)
records.nuance: 廊下 is a hallway or corridor inside a building. 廊下は走らないでください is a polite prohibition against running there.
records.logic: 廊下は sets the place as the topic; 走らないでください means please do not run.
records.difference: 廊下 is an indoor corridor; 道（みち） is a road or path.

records.nuance: 瓶（びん） is a glass bottle or jar. 瓶ビール is beer served in a bottle; the sentence says one was ordered.
records.logic: 瓶ビール specifies bottled beer; を注文した means ordered it.
records.difference: 瓶 is a bottle/jar; 缶（かん） is a can.

records.nuance: 褒める means praise or commend someone. Here the person was praised because they worked hard; the Japanese does not specify who worked hard, while the deck English adds “he.”
records.logic: 頑張ったので褒められました means “because [someone] worked hard, [they] were praised”; Japanese leaves both subjects implicit.
records.difference: 褒める is praise; 叱る（しかる） is scold.

records.kanji_breakdown:
元 = beginning
旦 = dawn; morning
records.nuance: 元旦 strictly refers to New Year’s morning; it is also commonly used for January 1 as a whole. Here the card dates the New Year card’s arrival to Jan. 1; the exact time of day is not certain.
records.logic: 元旦に sets the arrival time/date; 彼から年賀状が来た says a New Year card came from him.
records.meaning: New Year’s morning; New Year’s Day (common usage)
records.difference: 元旦 is New Year’s morning (also commonly the whole day); 元日（がんじつ） is January 1 as a full day.

records.nuance: 袖 means a sleeve of clothing. このシャツは袖が短い says the shirt has short sleeves; it is about sleeve length, not shirt length.
records.logic: 袖が短い describes the sleeves as short.
records.difference: 袖 is a sleeve; 襟（えり） is a collar.

records.nuance: 長袖 means long sleeves or a long-sleeved garment. Here the speaker wore one because it was cold; “shirt” is specified in English but not in the Japanese.
records.logic: 長袖を着ました means wore long-sleeved clothing; 着る is used for upper-body garments.
records.difference: 長袖 has long sleeves; 半袖（はんそで） has short sleeves.
records.filipino: mahahabang manggas; damit na mahaba ang manggas

records.nuance: 半袖 means short sleeves or a short-sleeved garment. Here the speaker suggests wearing a short-sleeved shirt today.
records.logic: 半袖のシャツ identifies a short-sleeved shirt; 着よう is a volitional “let’s/I’ll wear.”
records.difference: 半袖 has short sleeves; 長袖（ながそで） has long sleeves.
records.filipino: maikling manggas; damit na maikli ang manggas

records.kanji_breakdown: 馬鹿 = foolish; stupid (whole-word meaning; conventional spelling)
records.nuance: 馬鹿 means foolish or stupid. 私は馬鹿だった is self-critical (“I was foolish”); when directed at another person, it can be insulting.
records.logic: 私は馬鹿だった evaluates the speaker’s past self; だった is past tense.
records.difference: 馬鹿 is blunt and can insult someone; 愚か（おろか） is a more formal “foolish.”

records.nuance: 凄い can mean amazing, tremendous, or intense. With rain, 凄い雨 means very heavy/intense rain; the English “raining cats and dogs” is an idiom, not a literal meaning.
records.logic: 凄い雨になった says the rain became intense/heavy; なる marks a change of state.
records.difference: 凄い is an emphatic “amazing/intense”; 激しい（はげしい） specifically means intense/violent.

records.nuance: 剃る means shave hair with a razor. Here the father shaves his beard every day; 髭 refers to facial hair.
records.logic: 髭を剃る is the ordinary expression for shaving facial hair.
records.difference: 剃る is shave with a razor; 刈る（かる） means cut/clip hair or grass.

records.nuance: 喧嘩 means a quarrel or fight, verbal or physical depending on context. 喧嘩はやめて is a direct request to stop fighting.
records.logic: 喧嘩はやめて makes the fighting the thing to stop; やめて is a direct casual request.
records.difference: 喧嘩 is a quarrel/fight; 口論（こうろん） specifically means a verbal argument.

records.nuance: 叩く can mean tap, strike, or hit with the hand or an object. Here the father struck the child’s bottom; the English “slapped” is one contextual interpretation of this general verb.
records.logic: 子供のおしりを叩いた means he hit/tapped the child on the bottom; を marks the part struck.
records.difference: 叩く means hit/tap; 拍手する（はくしゅする） means clap one’s hands.

records.nuance: 噛む means bite or chew. With food understood from context, “chew more thoroughly” is intended; the command asks the listener to chew better.
records.logic: もっとよく噛みなさい means “chew more thoroughly”; もっとよく modifies how the listener chews.
records.difference: 噛む means bite/chew; 飲み込む（のみこむ） means swallow.

records.kanji_breakdown:
味噌 = miso
汁 = soup; broth
records.nuance: 味噌汁 is miso soup, a soup seasoned with miso paste. Here the speaker drinks/eats it every day; 飲む is used in Japanese for soup.
records.logic: 味噌汁を飲みます describes the daily habit; 毎日 marks frequency.
records.difference: 味噌汁 is soup seasoned with miso; お吸い物（おすいもの） is a clear broth soup.

records.nuance: 姪（めい） means a sibling’s daughter. Japanese does not mark number here, so the sentence may refer to one niece or more; the English deck translation uses “nieces.”
records.logic: 姪 identifies a kinship relationship: the daughter of one's sibling. 私の establishes the relationship to the speaker. The noun itself does not specify whether one niece or several nieces are meant.
records.difference: 姪 is a niece; 甥（おい） is a nephew.

records.nuance: 苺（いちご） is a strawberry. Here this strawberry is described as very sweet.
records.logic: この苺 identifies this strawberry, and とても甘い describes its taste.
records.difference: 苺 is a strawberry; 桃（もも） is a peach.

records.nuance: 茄子（なす） is eggplant/aubergine. Here it was eaten as tempura for dinner; Japanese does not say how many pieces.
records.logic: 茄子の天ぷら identifies eggplant tempura; 夕飯に places it at dinner.
records.difference: 茄子 is eggplant; 胡瓜（きゅうり） is cucumber.

records.nuance: 逢う（あう） means meet or see someone; this spelling can give a personal or emotionally significant tone, though the exact difference from 会う is not fixed in every context. Here he finally met a wonderful woman.
records.logic: 素晴らしい女性に逢えた means he was able to meet a wonderful woman at last; に marks the person met.
records.difference: 逢う and 会う both mean meet; 逢う can feel more personal or literary, while 会う is the usual general spelling.

records.kanji_breakdown:
椅 = chair
子 = object suffix (word cue)
records.nuance: 椅子（いす） is a chair. Here the elderly person sat down on one; お年寄り is a respectful term for an older person.
records.logic: 椅子に座った means sat on a chair; に marks the place/surface sat on.
records.difference: 椅子 is a chair; ソファ is a sofa/couch.

records.nuance: 痩せる is intransitive: become thinner or lose weight. Here the speaker says they lost a little weight; the sentence does not say whether it was intentional.
records.logic: 少し痩せました says the speaker became a little thinner/lost some weight.
records.difference: 痩せる is become thin/lose weight; 痩せさせる means make someone lose weight.

records.nuance: 箸（はし） are chopsticks. 箸を上手に使える says the speaker can use them skillfully; よ can add explanatory emphasis.
records.logic: 箸を使える means be able to use chopsticks; 上手に describes skill.
records.difference: 箸 are chopsticks; フォーク is a fork.

records.nuance: 糊（のり） is glue or paste, often paper glue. Here it was used to stick two sheets of paper together.
records.logic: 糊で marks the adhesive used; 2枚の紙を貼り合わせた means the two sheets were pasted together.
records.difference: 糊 is adhesive/paste; テープ is adhesive tape.

records.nuance: 醤油（しょうゆ） is soy sauce, a fermented seasoning used in Japanese cooking. 足してください asks politely to add some more; the object is understood from context.
records.logic: もう少し means a little more; 醤油 is what the listener is asked to add.
records.difference: 醤油 is soy sauce; 味噌（みそ） is fermented soybean paste.

records.nuance: 鋏（はさみ） means scissors. この鋏はよく切れる says these scissors cut well or are sharp; 切れる is intransitive here.
records.logic: よく切れる describes the scissors’ cutting ability, not a person cutting something now.
records.difference: 鋏 are scissors; ナイフ is a knife.

records.nuance: 鞄（かばん） is a bag, case, or satchel. Here the black bag is the speaker’s; “briefcase” in English is more specific than the Japanese.
records.logic: その黒い鞄は僕のです identifies the black bag as belonging to the speaker.
records.difference: 鞄 is a general bag/case; 財布（さいふ） is a wallet.

records.nuance: 顎（あご） can refer to the jaw or chin. Here the speaker says the jaw/chin area hurts; Japanese does not identify a more exact part.
records.logic: 顎が痛い states that the jaw/chin hurts; が marks the part in pain.
records.difference: 顎 is the jaw/chin; 頬（ほお） is the cheek.

records.nuance: 飴（あめ） means candy or sweets, often hard candy. Here candies are inside a can; this reading is distinct from 雨（あめ）, “rain.”
records.logic: 缶に飴が入っています says candy is in the can; 入っている describes the contents.
records.difference: 飴 is candy; チョコレート is chocolate.

records.nuance: 石鹸（せっけん） means soap. 石鹸で手を洗う means wash one’s hands with soap.
records.logic: 石鹸で marks what is used to wash the hands; ください makes it a polite request.
records.difference: 石鹸 is soap, usually a bar; ハンドソープ is liquid hand soap.

records.nuance: 差 means a difference, gap, or disparity. Here it is the large income gap between the urban center and regional areas; 地方 need not mean only rural villages.
records.logic: 都心と地方では sets up the two areas for comparison; 収入に大きな差がある says income differs greatly.
records.difference: 差 is a difference/gap; 違い（ちがい） is a general difference or distinction.

records.nuance: 失う means lose or be deprived of something important. Here he lost a parent or parents in an earthquake; Japanese 親 does not specify the number, though the deck English uses “parents.”
records.logic: 地震で marks the cause/context, and 親を失いました means he lost his parents.
records.difference: 失う is lose something/someone; 無くす（なくす） commonly means misplace or lose an object.
records.filipino: mawalan; nawalan siya ng magulang dahil sa lindol

records.nuance: 外れる is intransitive: come off, detach, or be out of place. In this negative sentence, the jar lid will not come off.
records.logic: びんのふたが外れません means the lid does not come off; が marks the part that would detach.
records.meaning: to come off; detach; be out of place
records.difference: 外れる is detach/come off; 外す（はずす） is transitive, remove/detach something.

records.nuance: 測る means measure a physical dimension such as length, height, depth, or distance. Here the door’s height is to be measured.
records.logic: ドアの高さを測ってください asks for the door’s height to be measured.
records.difference: 測る is measure dimensions; 量る（はかる） is commonly weigh or measure volume.

records.nuance: 含める is transitive: include someone or something in a group or total. Here the ten participants include the speaker.
records.logic: 私を含めて10人 means ten people in total, counting the speaker.
records.difference: 含める is actively include; 含む（ふくむ） is contain/include as a property or component.

records.nuance: 含む means contain or include. Here the food contains a harmful substance; 有害 means harmful, while the English “poisonous” is stronger and less exact.
records.logic: その食品は有害物質を含んでいる says the food contains a harmful substance.
records.difference: 含む means contain/include; 含める is the transitive act of including something in a set.

records.kanji_breakdown: 頂戴 = please give me; receive (humble expression)
records.nuance: 頂戴（ちょうだい） is a humble expression meaning receive or “please give me.” それ、ひとつ頂戴 is an informal request for one of those.
records.logic: ひとつ頂戴 means “give me one, please”; the object is the thing being offered.
records.difference: 頂戴 is a humble/request form; ください is a more standard polite “please give.”
records.filipino: pahingi ng isa; maaari bang makahingi
